text_normalised: A narrative is a culturally embedded account that specifies means, activities, and attainments through which individuals can achieve or restore personal significance—the desire to matter, be respected, and have social worth. Narratives identify which actions are significance-promoting within a given cultural context. In situations where an individual's social identity is perceived as threatened, narratives may prescribe radical or violent actions as appropriate responses. Narratives function to guide individuals' quests for significance by delineating culturally recognized pathways to valued status. Social networks play a role in validating narratives and rewarding adherence to them, thereby reinforcing the prescribed actions and their perceived legitimacy within the community.

text: Indeed, as Kruglanski et al. (2019) explain in their 3N model of radicalization, the network (the third ÒNÓ) empowers the individuals who act in accordance with the radical narrative, instills in them the confidence of doing the right thing, and lends them the coveted status of heroes or martyrs. The 3N model of radicalization (Kruglanski et al., 2019) posits that radicalization results from the confluence of the need for significance, the narrative, and the network. The need for significance is the desire to matter, be respected, and have social worth (Kruglanski et al., 2022). When activated to a high degree, either by a significance loss (through a perceived humiliation, injustice, discrimination, or neglect) or by an opportunity for a significance gain, it evokes a quest for significance, and a search for ways of attaining or restoring significance. Such means of gaining significance are typically specified in a cultural narrative about activities and attainments that are significance promoting. In certain contexts, where the individualÕs social identity (nation, ethnicity, religion) is threatened by some real or imagined enemies, radical actionsÑoften violent in natureÑare part and parcel of such a significance-promoting narrative. The social network plays an important role in validating the narrative and rewards with significance those who adhere to it. In this sense, the network is critical to the radicalization process, as well as to the process of deradicalization. p. 991  The power of the network, in other words, is to push individual adherents to a violent extremist narrative to act on behalf of that narrative. P. 991  Individuals who make sacrifices for the groupÕs benefit, that is, act in accordance with the groupÕs value narratives, are rewarded with statusÑthat is, significance in Kruglanski et al.Õs (2019, 2022) conceptualizationÑthus incentivizing them to continue sacrificing for the sake of the group (Willer, 2009). p. 992  Nonetheless, it is possible that it is not the sheer presence or absence of a network that distinguishes lone actors from those who act in groups, but rather the value that these individuals place on networks, particularly in comparison to the value that they place on value-laden narratives that offer a road to significance. p. 993  Our theory, an expansion of the 3N model of radicalization (Kruglanski et al., 2019), posits two individual-level factors and two group-level factors that affect the relative value individuals place on networks (i.e., social influence and group processes) as compared to narratives (i.e., ideological arguments). p. 993  Because ambitious people desire the greatest significance, they are likely to place less value on the rewards promised by their local network than less ambitious people do. Rather, in their quest for maximal significance, highly ambitious people are wont to transcend their local network and rather derive their significance from adherence to the abstract narrative whose scope and reach is broader than their current network. pp. 993-994  Outside of the realm of violent extremism, peripheral members of fraternities and sororities have been found to be more likely to self-sacrifice on behalf of the group than central members, who may feel that the groupÕs respect for them is gotten because of their adherence to and representation of the value narrative rather than because of their sacrificing themselves for the group (Goldman & Hogg, 2016). p. 994  Speckhard et al. (2022) demonstrated that most interviewees in their sample of current and former White supremacists had never even been exposed to extremist narratives prior to joining their groups! Surely, these individuals require the Òideological guidanceÓ of a network (Bright et al., 2020, p. 503) so that they know how to best serve the narrative and attain significance. p. 994  Nevertheless, if both social and ideological factors (i.e., network and narrative) contribute to deradicalization, then both should be components of a successful deradicalization program (Kruglanski et al., 2014). p. 996
text_normalised: A narrative is a culturally embedded account that specifies means of attaining or restoring social significance through particular activities and attainments. It provides ideological arguments and value-laden content that define what actions are significance-promoting within a given context. Narratives can designate certain behaviours—including, in some contexts, radical or violent actions—as pathways to mattering, being respected, and having social worth. They function as abstract frameworks whose scope and reach may transcend local social networks, offering individuals a road to significance through adherence to their prescriptions. Narratives are validated and reinforced by social networks, which reward those who act in accordance with them. They serve as ideological guidance, informing individuals how to serve collective values and achieve significance. Narratives thus operate as cultural schemas that link specific conduct to the fulfilment of significance needs.

text: Though every proposed definition offers some insight into the inherent qualities that narratives possess, we follow Braddock and Dillard (2016, p. 447) to define a narrative as Òany cohesive, causally linked series of events that takes place in a dynamic world subject to conflict, transformation, and resolution through non-habitual, purposeful action performed by characters.Ó p. 2  we define narrative vividness independent of the outcomes that messages produce or their interdependence with audiences at which messages are aimed. Specifically, and similar to Keller and Block (1997), we define vividness as the degree to which a message is specific about individuals, their actions, the contexts in which those actions occur, and the actionsÕ outcomes in the story. In an illustrative example, an experimental manipulation by Smith and Schaffer (2000) contrasted Òan increase in the probability of an accidentÓ (nonvivid condition) with Òa high risk of bloody, bone-crushing accidentsÓ (vivid condition; p. 777). p. 2  Terrorists use several strategies to communicate with audiences and promote the adoption of their ideologies. One the most popular is the distribution of narratives containing themes consistent with the groupÕs ideology (Braddock and Horgan, 2016). p. 3  Research on terrorist communication has shown that these narratives are effective vehicles for promoting the assimilation of extremist beliefs, attitudes, and intentions that can ultimately lead to engagement in violent behavior (e.g., Braddock, 2015). Taken together, the persuasive potency of narratives (Braddock and Dillard, 2016) and the ubiquity of terrorist narratives that prompt psychological processes that contribute to radicalization (Corman, 2011; Furlow and Goodall, 2011) suggest that Òexposure to terrorist narratives can at least theoretically increase an individualÕs risk for supporting terrorismÓ (Braddock and Horgan, 2016, p. 385). p. 3  To explore how narcissism, Machiavellianism, subclinical psychopathy, and everyday sadism moderate the effects of features of narratives, it is important to first review the nature of these personality traits as well as their theorized association with support for terrorism. p. 3 (Note. here is talks about features of narratives. to this point there has been no real explicit discussion of what these features are.)  Terrorist narratives often depict explicit acts of violence against purported enemies of the group in great detail... The detail associated with depictions like these may provide everyday sadists with feelings of pleasure or excitement that render them more likely to be persuaded by the narrative. p. 6  the graphic nature of vivid terrorist narrative propaganda may be more appealing to those with subclinical psychopathic tendencies. This may be particularly true if the narrative depicts violent treatment of enemies in a graphic way. p. 6  The subtle differences in how video-based narratives are processed relative to text (see Shen et al., 2015; Braddock and Dillard, 2016), coupled with the fact that most terrorist narratives are consumed via engagement with content on interactive digital media (Ashraf, 2021), demands that future work in this domain evaluate potential interactions between personality traits like the Dark Tetrad and video-based terrorist narrative processing to evaluate persuasive efficacy. For instance, personality traits that favor intense visual stimuli may respond differently under these conditions. p. 14  the victimization of the extremist groupÕs adopted constituents (i.e., civilians in HLA territory)Ñis a common theme in the narrative propaganda of a wide variety of groups. To be sure, several researchers have shown that perceptions of victimization increase oneÕs vulnerability of radicalization to violence (see Maly et al., 2013; Braddock, 2015; Kharroub, 2015; Van Den Bos, 2018; Jensen et al., 2020). p. 14  in real-world scenarios, it is likely an individualÕs affinity for the source of a terrorist narrative would affect the persuasiveness of that narrative. Consider, for example, that terrorist narratives are often designed to elicit feelings of sympathy and perceptions of similarity and inclusion with the group that produces the message (see Corman and Schiefelbein, 2008; Corman, 2011). These outcomes are closely related to the persuasive efficacy of strategic messaging, meaning that without naming the author of the propaganda, there is no group to which audiences can feel sympathy, perceive similarity, or imagine inclusion. p. 14
text_normalised: A narrative is any cohesive, causally linked series of events that takes place in a dynamic world subject to conflict, transformation, and resolution through non-habitual, purposeful action performed by characters. Narratives possess inherent qualities that enable them to function as vehicles for communication and persuasion. They may contain themes consistent with particular ideologies and can depict events, actions, and outcomes with varying degrees of specificity regarding individuals, their actions, the contexts in which those actions occur, and the consequences of those actions. Narratives can be presented through different media formats, including text and video, and their processing may vary accordingly. They are capable of eliciting emotional responses and perceptions in audiences, and their persuasive efficacy may be influenced by audience characteristics and the relationship between audiences and narrative sources.

text_normalised: A narrative is any cohesive, causally linked series of events that takes place in a dynamic world subject to conflict, transformation, and resolution through non-habitual, purposeful action performed by characters. Narratives constitute a form of communication characterized by their sequential structure, wherein events are connected through causal relationships rather than presented as isolated occurrences. The narrative unfolds within a world that undergoes change, featuring conflicts that require resolution. This resolution emerges through deliberate, non-routine actions undertaken by characters who populate the narrative world. The defining features include causal coherence among events, dynamic transformation of the narrative world, the presence of conflict requiring resolution, and purposeful character action that deviates from habitual behavior.

text: Previous research in the TurkishÐKurdish conflict  context highlighted two opposing conflict narratives  endorsed by different groups: (a) a terrorism narrative,  which describes the problem as stemming mainly from  the PKK and foreign powers, and (b) an independence  narrative, which describes the problem as a need for  independence for Kurds. (Page 76)
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that describes and frames a social or political problem by identifying its primary sources and nature. Narratives can be oppositional, with different groups endorsing competing accounts of the same situation. Each narrative selectively emphasizes particular causal agents, attributions, and problem definitions while potentially minimizing or excluding alternative explanations. Through this framing process, narratives shape how groups understand conflicts and issues by providing coherent interpretations that highlight specific actors, motivations, and circumstances as central to explaining events or conditions. Different narratives may coexist within the same context, reflecting divergent group perspectives and interests regarding the fundamental character and origins of shared problems or disputes.

text: According to this model, the path to radicalization begins with the activation of the significance quest, which directs attention to the means of achieving significanceÑa passionate need to count, to be someone, to be recognized, to matter. These means are found in the collective narrative (ideology) of the ingroup as it is the beliefs of a group that inform what is meaningful or important in the eyes of others. If such an ideology identifies violence and terrorism as the only means to achieve significance, people may support and engage in violence and terrorism (page 2)
text_normalised: Narrative is a collective ideological framework held by an ingroup that specifies the means through which members can achieve significance and recognition. It consists of shared beliefs that define what is considered meaningful or important within the group's value system. The narrative directs individuals' attention toward particular pathways for mattering and being recognized by others. It identifies and legitimates specific courses of action as appropriate or necessary means to fulfill the quest for significance. When a narrative designates certain behaviors—including extreme actions—as the exclusive or primary route to achieving importance, it shapes members' understanding of available options and can motivate their engagement in those behaviors. The narrative thus functions as an interpretive lens through which group members understand their possibilities for gaining recognition and fulfilling their need to count as someone significant.

text: "Another reason why conspiracy beliefs might affect interpersonal relationships is peopleÕs evaluation of the endorsement of conspiracy theories. Conspiracy theories are commonly regarded as flawed narratives that are believed by marginal social groups (Barkun, 2015). An example of this negative perception is peopleÕs frequent association of conspiracy beliefs with mental instability and problems of mental health (Green et al., 2023; Klein et al., 2015; Sparkman, 2012). Although conspiracy beliefs positively correlate with some clinical traits (e.g., paranoia, schizotypy; Darwin et al., 2011), they are clearly distinct phenomena (Alsuhibani et al., 2022; Imhoff & Lamberty, 2018). Another example is peopleÕs tendency to make use of the label Òconspiracy theoryÓ to refer to events they disbelieve (Douglas et al., 2021), which reflects the stigmatizing value of such a label. Furthermore, people anticipate that the endorse- ment of conspiracy theories entails social costs, like being negatively evaluated and socially excluded (Green et al., 2023; Lantian et al., 2018). Taken together, these findings suggest that belief in conspiracy theories is largely stigmatized."
text_normalised: Narratives are structured accounts or explanatory frameworks that can be evaluated as flawed or credible by observers. They function as belief systems that individuals or groups endorse to interpret events or phenomena. Narratives may be subject to social evaluation, where their acceptance or rejection reflects broader perceptions of their validity, coherence, or alignment with mainstream understanding. When narratives are perceived as flawed, they may carry stigmatizing associations, leading observers to attribute negative characteristics to those who endorse them. Narratives thus operate within social contexts where their content and the act of endorsing them can influence interpersonal judgments, social positioning, and the perceived legitimacy of the beliefs they convey. The evaluation of narratives involves assessments of their explanatory adequacy and the social standing of those who accept them.

text: The approach defines a narrative as Ôa construction of sequence or consequenceÕ (Taylor, 2010, p. 36) in talk. In other words, narratives contain a temporal reference and cause-andeffect relationship. However, differentiating from narrative research, the analytic focus of the approach is not only on the content of the talk but also on what is accomplished in the talk Ð how and why it is told in a particular situation. Consequently, according to the narrativeÐdiscursive approach, a narrative is not a recollection of a moment from the past but a medium that people use for discursive and rhetorical purposes in social interaction, such as interviews (page 497)
text_normalised: A narrative is a construction of sequence or consequence in talk, containing temporal reference and cause-and-effect relationships. Rather than being a recollection of a moment from the past, a narrative functions as a medium that people use for discursive and rhetorical purposes in social interaction. The focus extends beyond the content of what is told to encompass what is accomplished through the telling—how and why it is narrated in a particular situation. Narratives thus serve as tools through which speakers achieve specific interactional goals, constructing meaning and performing social actions within communicative contexts.

text: "Discourse analysis is combined with narrative analysis to show how Incels use specific language to narrate, and therefore make sense of, their lived experiences.41 Individuals act as storytellers who interpret their experiences through words and then organise those words into narratives, endowing those experiences with meaning.42 In the process, they create a particular social order within, and inherent to, their worldview.43 This social order indicates perceived understandings of power relations and forms the basis for political ideology. If politics can be understood as Òa struggle for power, between those who seek to assert and maintain their power and those who seek to resist it . . .Ó44 then narratives Òhelp us understand ourselves as political beings . . . . Insofar as narratives affect our perceptions of political reality, which in turn affects our actions in response to or in anticipation of political events, narrative plays a critical role in the construction of political behavior.Ó45 Here it must be noted that narratives represent particular political identities and ideologies but do not necessarily reflect an objective Òpolitical reality.Ó46 Narrative research is particularly useful in the study of Incels because of its sensitivity to positionality and the related political implications.47 Narratives which emphasise positionality, as Incel narratives do, focus on relations of power i.e., who has power and who does not. In most narratives, actors attempt to seize the dominant position to leverage or challenge the existing narrative.48 In the case of Incels, however, their narrative places them in the position of the victim or the oppressed. In doing so, Incels have created a counternarrative to the dominant hegemonic masculinities that are generally seen as driving the existing social order.49"
text_normalised: Narratives are organised interpretations through which individuals make sense of their lived experiences by structuring words into meaningful accounts. Through this process, narrators create a particular social order inherent to their worldview, indicating perceived understandings of power relations and forming the basis for political ideology. Narratives help individuals understand themselves as political beings; insofar as they affect perceptions of political reality, which in turn affects actions in response to or in anticipation of political events, narratives play a critical role in constructing political behaviour. Narratives represent particular political identities and ideologies but do not necessarily reflect objective political reality. They are sensitive to positionality and emphasise relations of power—who has power and who does not. Actors within narratives typically attempt to seize dominant positions to leverage or challenge existing narratives, though some narratives position actors as victims or oppressed, creating counternarratives to dominant social orders.

text: "The grandiose self-image of the Proud Boys is entangled politically with a hypersensitivity to threats, real or imagined. Rather than a secondary byproduct of their self-image, threat narratives go to the core of their collective identity as innocent victims to the existential dangers that Òpure AmericansÓ face from various enemies. In general, threat narratives advanced by conflict actors tend to follow a familiar pattern as follows: Our adversaries have harmed our people in the past; they continue to threaten us, and we are their perennial targets." (Page 546)
text_normalised: Threat narratives are accounts advanced by conflict actors that follow a characteristic pattern: they assert that adversaries have harmed the group in the past, continue to pose ongoing dangers, and persistently target the group. These narratives are central to collective identity formation, positioning the group as innocent victims facing existential threats from designated enemies. Rather than being secondary to group self-conception, threat narratives constitute a core component of how the collective understands itself in relation to perceived dangers. They reflect a hypersensitivity to threats, whether real or imagined, and serve to define the group's relationship to adversaries and the nature of the dangers it confronts.

text: The grandiose self-image of the Proud Boys is entangled politically with a hypersensitivity to threats, real or imagined. Rather than a secondary byproduct of their self-image, threat narratives go to the core of their collective identity as innocent victims to the existential dangers that Òpure AmericansÓ face from various enemies. In general, threat narratives advanced by conflict actors tend to follow a familiar pattern as follows: Our adversaries have harmed our people in the past; they continue to threaten us, and we are their perennial targets. The scope of their perceived threats is wide-ranging. Consider the following threat narratives advanced by the Proud Boys: ¥ Europe is engaged in a war to preserve the Judeo-Christian heritage in the face of the increasing numbers of Muslims (Wilson, 2017). ¥ Western civilization is experiencing a war against non- Westerners (Wilson, 2017). ¥ Multicultural groups are dangerous to the United States and the world (Kenes, 2021). ¥ Democrats are communists who seek to destroy freedoms in the United States. ¥ China seeks to become the greatest military power and dominate the United States. p. 546  These threat narratives are filled with dehumanizing images of non-Westerner population groups. p. 546  Such narcissism is manifested in four sorts of narratives: (a) grandiosity, (b) threat, (c) denigration, and (d) righteous rage. Each narrative pattern functions as a cognitiveÐ emotive force of the extremistsÕ mindset, that is, a potentiality and readiness to act in certain ways. text_normalised: Threat narratives are accounts advanced by conflict actors that follow a characteristic pattern: adversaries have harmed the in-group in the past, continue to threaten them presently, and position the in-group as perennial targets. These narratives identify existential dangers facing the in-group from various enemies, with the scope of perceived threats potentially wide-ranging across different domains. Threat narratives form a core component of collective identity, framing the in-group as innocent victims. They may contain dehumanizing images of out-groups and function as a cognitive-emotive force within the mindset of those who advance them, representing a potentiality and readiness to act in certain ways. The salience of threat narratives varies in intensity, frequency, and impact according to changing social-political conditions.

text: "The most striking feature of the discourse of the Jonestown death tape is the amount of work Jones and his congregants put into their deliberation about what course of action was required in the situation they confronted. The analysis makes a compelling case that the chosen response of extreme violence did not flow naturally from their unmet needs and vulnerabilities or the objective conditions of the social reality they faced. Rather, their response was debated and justified in discourse and persuasive commu- nication that mobilized the group to action. Our analysis has shown how this was done in two moves. First, the identity of the group, a foremost concern, was developed in talking about the reality of their situation. The collective experience of persecution and deep mistrust in the US government (as well as the salvation offered by Jones) is reworked into a narrative of present hopelessness. After the murder of the senator, their powerful enemies would no longer Ôleave us aloneÕ. They were a powerless minority. Second, this narrative of unique circumstances and hopelessness informed the narrated need for drastic action. Alternative courses of action were proposedÑappeal to Russia, revolutionary suicideÑand contrasted with unacceptable alternatives, being killed Ôlike the JewsÕ or subsumed back into the system as ÔdummiesÕ. Critically, the distinction between acceptable and unacceptable action is framed in terms of group identity as socialist, revolutionary outsiders. The discourse creates a narrative fit between identity and action."
text_normalised: Narrative is a discursive construction through which groups interpret their situation and justify courses of action. It is developed through deliberation and persuasive communication that mobilizes collective response. Narrative involves reworking collective experiences and circumstances into a coherent account of present conditions and future possibilities. It establishes connections between group identity and appropriate action by framing situations in terms that make certain responses appear necessary or acceptable while rendering alternatives unacceptable. Narrative does not flow naturally from objective conditions or unmet needs but is actively produced through discourse that shapes how reality is understood. It creates coherence between who the group understands itself to be and what actions follow from that identity, establishing what can be termed narrative fit between identity and action. Through this process, narrative functions to organize collective understanding and guide group behaviour in response to perceived circumstances.

text: Politicians utilize discourse to create public norms and values needed to rationalize government action and mobilize public support against the perceived enemy (Altheide & Grimes, 2011; Berinsky, 2007; Mackay, 2015). During intrastate social clashes, politicians generate public patronage by identifying themselves as part of the masses and tapping popular collective emotions (Montiel & Uyheng, 2020; Obradovi_, Power, & Sheehy-Skeffington, 2020). In addition, leadersÕ talk can shape their constituentsÕ view of reality, by focusing on national issues that emphasize social cleavages against a perceived public enemy (Obradovi_ et al., 2020). These discursively constructed social fractures promote binary lenses in viewing a divided world inclined to dispute eruption. (Page 520)  We posit that discursive agents swell narratives by employing discursive strategies that sequentially transform, destroy, construct, and perpetuate talks over time. These tactical discourses aim to achieve a specific social, political, psychological, or linguistic goal (page 520)
text_normalised: Narratives are discursively constructed accounts that politicians and other agents employ to create public norms and values, rationalize action, and mobilize support. These constructions shape constituents' views of reality by emphasizing social cleavages and identifying perceived enemies, thereby promoting binary perspectives of a divided world. Narratives are generated through sequential discursive strategies that transform, destroy, construct, and perpetuate discourse over time. Agents utilize these tactical discourses to achieve specific social, political, psychological, or linguistic goals, often by identifying with the masses and tapping collective emotions to generate public patronage during social conflicts.

text: "In addition to the need for significance, further development of the SQT, the 3N model (Kruglanski et al., 2018, 2022), proposes two other variables influencing violent extremism: narrative and network. Although the need for significance is universal, the means to satisfy such a need are contextually dependent and identified in a narrative supported and vali- dated by oneÕs network (Kruglanski et al., 2022). Hence, dif- ferently from other needs, to which the response is intuitive (e.g., if one is hungry, one knows that the behavior allowing one to satisfy this need is to eat), the response to the need for significance is socially acquired (Kruglanski et al., 2022). Among the various means to reach/restore significance, it is the subscription to a radical narrative, depicting violence as the appropriate means, and the affiliation with a radical net- work supporting such a narrative, that will guide action toward violent extremism (Kruglanski et al., 2018, 2022). In terms of narrative, based on past research on meaning in life, Kruglanski et al. (2018) argue that when one is in need for significance, one will look for an ideology that pro- vides a sense of confidence, allows one to understand the surrounding world, and defines the goals to pursue in the quest for significance. Subscribing to an ideology will pro- vide the individual with a sense of identity and significance. According to Kruglanski et al. (2017, 2018), individuals in need for significance are especially sensitive to a radical ide- ology depicting the use of violence, because violence is per- ceived as the Ògreat equalizerÓ capable of reverting the perceived asymmetry of power by causing pain to those con- ceived as enemies. Therefore, an individual subscribing to such an ideology will be more likely to engage in violent extremism as it is depicted as moral and acceptable. Finally, the network component of the 3N model refers to an affiliation with a radical group that shares the same beliefs and helps validate the narrative. These social groups might be informally (e.g., friends and family) or formally orga- nized (e.g., extremist organizations). In such a network, group members function as epistemic authorities (Kruglanski et al., 2005) promoting the use of violence as the sole means to reach significance. To gain respect and admiration or, in other words, significance, from such epistemic authorities, the individual will be strongly motivated to act according to the groupÕs norms and values and therefore to engage in vio- lent extremism."
text_normalised: A narrative is an ideology that provides individuals with a framework for understanding the world, defining goals, and constructing a sense of identity and significance. It is contextually dependent and socially acquired, offering guidance on the means to satisfy psychological needs rather than intuitive responses. Narratives supply confidence and clarity about one's surroundings and prescribe courses of action aligned with particular values or beliefs. When individuals subscribe to a narrative, it shapes their perception of appropriate behaviour and moral acceptability. The narrative functions as a cognitive structure that interprets social reality and legitimates specific actions as meaningful or justified within that interpretive framework. Its influence depends on validation and support from social networks that share and reinforce the narrative's content and prescriptions.

text: Master narratives are Òdominant cultural storylines which form the context of (peopleÕs) livesÓ and are the means by which we understand our own stories and those of others, Òidentifying what is assumed to be a normative experienceÓ (page 1)
text_normalised: Narratives are dominant cultural storylines that form the context of people's lives and serve as the means by which individuals understand their own stories and those of others. They function to identify what is assumed to be a normative experience within a given cultural setting. These storylines provide an interpretive framework through which personal and collective experiences are made meaningful and comprehensible. By establishing normative expectations, narratives shape how individuals position themselves and others in relation to culturally shared understandings of experience.

text: "The focus on fantasy and fantasy narratives emphasizes how any search for ontologi- cal security is always a storyÑa fantasyÑthat can never be fulfilled, regardless of how powerful and real such stories can feel in terms of sense-making. In concrete terms, it means that individuals, groups, and even states respond to ontological insecurity by tem- porarily closing down categorical identifications. In StavrakakisÕ (1999) terms, it is a form of banal representational fantasy that works to defend against emotional anxieties and traumatic experiences." "White supremacy is a vague discourse centered around a fantasy in which White peo- ple and culture are intrinsically superior to those of other ethnicities and races. It implies a narrative in which common (fantasmatic) pasts and values are shared, and where White people are entitled to design, operationalize, and ontologically secure (e.g., through tra- ditions, policies, and laws) their survival, safety, and prosperity to the detriment of other genders, ethnicities, and racesÑoften through violent means (Oesteraas, 2022; Vander Zanden, 1959; Wu & Li, 2020)."
text_normalised: A narrative is a story that functions to provide ontological security by temporarily closing down categorical identifications in response to anxieties and traumatic experiences. It operates as a form of representational fantasy that defends against emotional disturbances through sense-making, even though the security it offers can never be fully realized. Narratives center around fantasies that construct shared pasts and values, establishing frameworks through which individuals, groups, or collectives understand their identities and positions. These stories work to secure existence and meaning despite their inherently unfulfillable nature, yet they can feel powerful and real to those who employ them. Narratives thus serve as mechanisms for managing insecurity by creating coherent accounts that temporarily stabilize identity categories and provide frameworks for action and understanding.

Desire ties together what Lacan refers to as the Imaginary, the Symbolic, and the Real (objet petit a) through images, language, and enjoyment (jouissance; Burgess, 2017; Lacan, 1988). text: "The 3N model (Kruglanski et al., 2019; Webber & Kruglanski, 2017) proposes that radicalization arises from the intersection of three psychological forces: need, narrative, and network. text: We see collective narratives as Ômeta-storiesÕ embraced by groups that incorporate values and beliefs about social reality, therefore providing a blueprint for group norms which, in turn, inform group members' behaviour. (Abstract)  Humans are Òmoral, believing, and narrating animalsÓ who thrive in the moral order created by shared stories Òabout who we are, what we ought to do, and what is sacredÓ (Haidt & Kesebir, 2010, p. 65; Smith, 2003). Throughout history, shared stories have shaped cultures and societies. These stories include collective narratives about the creation of the universe and the meaning of life which underpin various religions, interpretations of historical events, political thought, and conflict. As such, collective narratives play a key role in shaping individual identities (Hammack, 2008, 2011). As for their influence at a societal level, they have been used in explanations of intractable historical conflicts (Adisonmez, 2019; Bar-Tal, 1998, 2011) and polarisation on social issues of high public interest, such as climate change, Brexit, and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic (Bain et al., 2012; Hobolt et al., 2021; MacCarron et al., 2020). p.2  Narratives can be conceptualised at either an individual (personal) level or at a societal (collective) level. Individual narratives are seen as being embodied in the cultural practices that individuals take part in and represent a cognitive process of meaning making which helps people gain a sense of personal coherence (Hammack & Pilecki, 2012, p. 78). However, their function goes beyond that. When shared within and across groups, these narratives fulfil a need for collective solidarity through shared meaning (Hammack, 2008; Hammack & Pilecki, 2012). They incorporate beliefs about social categories and the relationships between them in society, reside in the collective memory of groups and are anchored in interpretations of history. They can take the form of cohesive stories about social reality, congruent with particular sets of values and systems of beliefs (Bliuc, Smith, & Moynihan, 2020), therefore, helping position the individual in a broader intergroup context. However, when they are contested across groups and within groups, they provide the bases of dissent, division, and conflict. p. 3  The functions of collective narratives in society can be categorised across two dimensions (as illustrated in Table 1): a) the (group level) context in which collective narratives develop and are sharedÑintergroup vs. intragroup; and b) the narrative driversÑdissent (diversity of opinion) versus consensus (homogeneity of opinion). By applying these dimensions to the concept of collective narratives, four categories of functions connected to different narrative types emerge: a) intergroup unification (collective narratives underpinning allyship and ingroup expansion); b) intragroup cohesion (collective narratives underpinning group efficacy and empowerment/influence); c) intergroup division (collective narratives underpinning the formation and evolution of ideologically opposed camps and conflict between these); and d) intragroup fragmentation (collective narratives underpinning schism, factionalisation, and radicalisation). Each of these narrative types can explain different types of behaviours: 1) (intergroup) unifying narratives are connected to cooperative, altruistic, and pro-social behaviours (e.g., contributions to end child poverty, etc.), 2) (ingroup) empowering narratives to collective action in social movements that gain momentum through attracting allies from across social categories and group memberships (e.g., Black Lives Matter), 3) (intergroup) divisive narratives to behaviours and collective action in line with competing social movements (e.g., pro-life vs. pro-choice, etc.), and 4) (ingroup) factionalising narratives to fringe or extreme behaviours by radicalised splinter sub-groups. It is important to note here that the application of this typology is highly-perspective dependent, so how a narrative is categorised would depend on the group membership of the social actor. This means that in a classic intergroup conflict context (between a disadvantaged minority and an advantaged majority), an empowering narrative from the perspective of the disadvantaged and allies' groups, could be seen as divisive by members of the advantaged majority. p. 6  Intergroup unificationÑunifying narratives underpinning cooperative behaviour. Narratives achieving intergroup unification are based on consensus that goes beyond group boundaries, so they come to be shared across social categories and group memberships. Because they highlight what unifies us as humans, they are connected to identification with superordinate, non-polarising social categories such as ÔhumanityÕ and speak to unifying emotions, such as compassion and care for those vulnerable. Because, in most cases, these narratives are based on universal principles and pro-social beliefs connected to the survival of us as a species, they speak to the most basic human values around cooperation. As a result, these narratives incorporate aspects of social reality on which people across groups, social categories, and political fault-lines can all agree onÑuniversal fears about human vulnerability in the face of the force of nature (i.e., the possibility of being obliterated by a tsunami or hurricane) is something shared across cultures and geo-political boundaries. Therefore, natural disasters even in remote parts of the world can elicit emotions which are consistent with moral values such as ingroup loyalty and care/harm. The driving narrative here incorporates calls to solidarity across group boundaries and endorses pro-social behaviour and cooperation, these narratives being often associated to benevolent support including acts of charitable giving and shows of empathy (Louis et al., 2019) as well as socio-political action in the form of allyship (Radke et al., 2020; Uysal et al., 2022; Van Leeuwen & Zagefka, 2017). p. 6-7  Intragroup cohesionÑempowering narratives underpinning group efficacy and collective action. This category of collective narratives may both reflect the existing consensus between ingroup members about core identity issues and function as further enhancers of that consensus. As a result, they can strengthen the group's internal cohesion. Because these narratives contain strong and often highly specific messages about a group's aims, core values, and its strength (i.e., much more specific than unifying intergroup narratives which naturally seek to broaden the ingroup support base with more generic/universal messaging) they can provide the bases for the formation and mobilisation of more targeted activism. p.7  Intergroup divisionÑdivisive narratives underpinning conflict. These narratives are based on dissent and develop when there are at least two opposing versions of social reality available; furthermore, these opposing versions should have the ability to appear as equally valid from the differing group's perspectives. They can be seen as mutually exclusive by the members of the groups in conflictÑthere is more than one story or interpretation of social reality, and they are both powerful in relatively equal degrees from different viewpoints. Because of this, these types of narratives are intrinsically polarising. Mutually exclusive narratives create conditions for the formation of ideologically opposed camps (Bliuc, Betts, et al., 2020, 2021). These narratives create ideal conditions for intergroup conflict and polarisation in the form of psychological and ideological distancing because they are based on mutually exclusive versions of social reality which are connected to norms and behaviours that aim to achieve competing group goals (Bliuc et al., 2021). The dichotomy between climate change deniers and believers clearly illustrates thisÑon the one hand climate change is seen as an urgent anthropogenic crisis that demands attention, and on the other it is dismissed as an exaggerated or even invented issue. These two views are mutually exclusive interpretations of recent climate phenomena and, furthermore, any increase in the number of deniers is a commensurate loss for consensus to mitigate climate change. Other examples of ideologically opposed camps that are mutually exclusive include asylum-seeker supporters and their opponents (Burke & Goodman, 2012) and pro-life and pro-choice supporters (John, 2017). p. 8  Intragroup fragmentationÑfactionalising narratives underpinning schism and radical behaviours. Fragmentation within groups stems from dissenting intragroup narratives on issues which are central to the group's social identity. These narratives can explain schisms in established groups, factionalisation, and radicalisation. In a sense, intragroup conflict can be conceptualised as driven by internal narrative differentiation; through intragroup deliberation and debate, group members refine the meaning of group identity, and as such, continuously refine and change the social identity content of a group. Research by Sani and colleagues (Sani, 2008; Sani & Reicher, 1998, 2000; Sani & Todman, 2002) shows how dissent about issues which are core to the group's identity can lead to schism within a group as for instance, within the Church of England. According to research on schism, one of the main bases for dissent within a group is the meaning attributed to the particular identity or social category (Sani & Todman, 2002). In other words, the meaning of a particular social identity can be contested within the groupÑone of the best illustrations of this process is provided by the many variations in the representation of nationhood within a national context. That is, within the same nation, representations that include recent immigrants to the country and representations that exclude them can co-exist (Pehrson et al., 2009; Reicher et al., 2006; Teichman & Bar-Tal, 2008). For example, in research by Pehrson et al. (2009), within one nation prejudice and discrimination on one hand, and openness to immigrants on the other, can align to different definitions of national identity (indicating intragroup fragmentation at the level of a nation). In the context of the Australian national identity, beliefs about social categories and the relationships between them were found to shape group behaviours including support for and opposition to racist riots (Bliuc et al., 2012). In this research, support and opposition to riots were aligned to different narratives about national identity: one incorporating values and beliefs typical to an Anglo-Saxon, White version of national identity and one incorporating inclusive narratives based on multicultural values. p. 9
text_normalised: Narratives are meta-stories embraced by groups that incorporate values and beliefs about social reality, providing a blueprint for group norms that inform members' behaviour. They represent cognitive processes of meaning-making that help individuals gain personal coherence while fulfilling needs for collective solidarity through shared meaning. Narratives incorporate beliefs about social categories and relationships between them in society, reside in collective memory, and are anchored in interpretations of history. They take the form of cohesive stories about social reality congruent with particular value sets and belief systems, positioning individuals within broader intergroup contexts. When shared within and across groups, narratives create consensus or dissent; when contested across or within groups, they provide bases for division and conflict. Narratives can operate at individual (personal) or societal (collective) levels, being embodied in cultural practices and shaping both individual identities and collective understanding of social reality.

text: "According to the Significance Quest Theory (SQT) and its 3N model, violent extremism is the endpoint of a process of radicalization triggered by a need for significance and nourished by the subscription to a radical nar- rative and the affiliation to a radical network validating such ideology (Kruglanski, Jasko, Webber, Chernikova, & Molinario, 2018). In this sense, violent extremism is the product of the following equation: Òneed + narrative + network = violent extremismÓ. It is important to note that, according to the theory, the quest for significance can also be activated by a perceived opportunity to gain significance and not only through significance loss (Kruglanski et al., 2018). However, to the best of our knowledge, only the recently published paper by Resta, Ellenberg, Kruglanski, and Pierro (2022) tested and confirmed this assumption. For this reason, the present research focuses on the need for significance as the main predictor of violent extremism. Specifically, the need for significance refers to a desire to be someone, to matter, and to have one's value acknowledged. It is con- ceived as a fundamental need triggered by a negative experience, such as discrimination, oppression, and humiliation (Kruglanski, Chen, Dechesne, Fishman, & Orehek, 2009). Once triggered, the need for significance leads to an obsessive passion/pursuit (Kruglanski et al., 2018; Vallerand et al., 2003) towards its satisfaction, namely the quest for significance. At this point, violence might be seen as an appealing path allowing the indi- vidual to reach significance, because of its potential for reversing asymmetrical power relations: those who feel attacked and hurt can inflict pain on their aggressors (Kruglanski, Chemikova, Dugas, Jasko, & Webber, 2017). According to the SQT and its model, this is especially true for those subscribing to a radical narrative blaming an individual or an outgroup for their own or their group's suffering. The radical narrative, therefore, identifies the enemy to be targeted and depicts the radical and violent means by which to do so. Such a radical ideology is passed on and validated by a radical group that can also function as a source of significance and acknowledg- ment of one's worth (Kruglanski et al., 2017). Subscribing to a radical ideology and affiliating with a radical group, when facing the need for significance, can lead to violent extremism. However, subscribing to, and affili- ating with, other (prosocial) narratives and groups can help the individual to find alternative (prosocial) means to reach significance (Kruglanski et al., 2017)."
text_normalised: A narrative is an ideological framework that individuals subscribe to, which provides explanations for experiences of suffering or grievance by identifying responsible parties and prescribing means of response. Narratives function to interpret social reality by attributing causality for negative experiences to specific individuals or outgroups and legitimising particular courses of action, which may be radical and violent or prosocial in nature. Such frameworks are transmitted and validated through group affiliation, serving to guide behaviour toward specific goals. Narratives operate as cognitive structures that shape how individuals understand their circumstances and determine appropriate responses, offering pathways through which fundamental psychological needs may be satisfied. The content and orientation of narratives—whether radical or prosocial—influence the nature of actions individuals pursue in response to motivational states.

text: "Narrative refers to the role of ideology (shared beliefs) in the choice of the way to find significance. Even though not all ideologies support the use of violence, some consider the use of violent means legitimate and effective. In turn, these ideologies provide moral justification, which impels disinhibition and the use of violence (Blanger et al., 2019; Kruglanski et al., 2013; Lobato et al., 2018). This type of narrative, which we can consider extremist, boosts the appeal of portraying the world in Manichaean or dualist terms (us vs them), leaving no room for ambiguity or cognitively demanding nuances. It also provides cognitive closure aimed at lowering uncertainty and restoring certainty (Webber et al., 2018). Narrative is where the person identifies the objectives and actions needed to find significance and obtain the moral justification that legitimizes violence against the out- group (Blanger et al., 2019). Therefore, we could say that a series of conditions must be met in order for violence to become an appropriate means to achieve significance. The narrative has to first identify an injustice, secondly identify a guilty party (the out- group) and thirdly justify violence as a legitimate and practically efficient way to make up for the injustice (Kruglanski et al., 2019). In this way, the narrative of political- religious terrorism may lower states of personal uncertainty and offer an opportunity to find or restore personal significance (Kruglanski et al., 2019)."
text_normalised: Narrative refers to a system of shared beliefs that guides individuals in selecting means to achieve significance. It provides moral justification that legitimizes particular courses of action, including potentially violent ones, by framing objectives and necessary steps. Narrative functions by identifying perceived injustices, attributing responsibility to specific parties, and establishing certain responses as legitimate and effective remedies. It often presents reality in binary terms, reducing ambiguity and cognitive complexity. Through this process, narrative offers cognitive closure that diminishes uncertainty and restores certainty for adherents. By delineating targets and justifying actions against them, narrative enables individuals to pursue significance through means that align with the ideological framework it articulates. The structure typically involves establishing a grievance, designating responsible agents, and validating specific responses as both morally justified and practically efficacious.

text: "Conflict narratives can be conceptualized as stories that frame the conflict, including its definitions, causes, and potential solutions. The way people see conflicts has consequences for conflict- and peace-related outcomes because they shape people's reactions to possible solutions to the conflict (e.g., Bar-Tal, 2013; Kaufman et al., 2003). Previous research in the Turkish-Kurdish conflict context (Ulu_ & Cohrs, 2016, 2017a) found two opposing conflict narratives: (a) a terrorism narrative (i.e., describes the conflict as stem- ming mainly from the armed wing of the minority group) and (b) an independence narrative (i.e., describes the conflict as a need for independence for the minority). It has been shown that these conflict narratives not only predict support for non-violent conflict resolution and aggressive policies but also can be gener- alized to other conflict contexts such as the Israeli-Palestine conflict (Ulu_, Lickel, et al., 2021). However, less attention has been given to the antecedents of conflict narratives such as identifying with an ingroup identity in an ethnopolitical conflict context. We argue that people's ingroup identities such as their reli- gious identities are particularly crucial in such contexts because it is on these identities conflicting parties form shared beliefs with respect to the conflict (Bar-Tal & Oren, 2000). In the current study, we aim to examine how conflict narratives may play an important role in the relationship between religious group identification (i.e., Catholic vs. Protestant) and willingness to forgive the other party for their wrongdo- ings during the conflict."
text_normalised: Narratives are stories that frame a conflict, including its definitions, causes, and potential solutions. They shape how people perceive conflicts and influence their reactions to possible resolutions and policy options. Narratives can take opposing forms that describe the same conflict differently, such as attributing it to armed actions by one group versus framing it as a struggle for independence. These narrative frameworks predict support for various conflict-related outcomes, including non-violent resolution approaches and aggressive policies. Narratives are shaped by antecedents such as ingroup identities, and conflicting parties form shared beliefs about the conflict based on these identities. Narratives can be generalised across different conflict contexts beyond their original setting.
