text: Relatedly, we rely on the importance of meaning-making frameworks to comprehend our own reality. These frameworks shape individualsÕ worldviews and values, as the foundations for their identities and life purposes (George & Park, 2016). For political extremists, subscription to an ideological narrative satisfies the need for significance through a commitment to a collective cause, even if the ideology professes the use of violence to garner respect, honor, and appreciation (page 1352)
text_normalised: Narratives are meaning-making frameworks that shape individuals' worldviews and values, serving as foundations for their identities and life purposes. They provide structures through which people comprehend their reality and establish their sense of self. Narratives can take ideological forms that individuals subscribe to, offering frameworks for understanding the world and one's place within it. Through commitment to these frameworks, narratives can satisfy psychological needs for significance by connecting individuals to collective causes and purposes. They function as organizing principles that give coherence to experience and provide direction for action and meaning in life.

text: "To illuminate how the two types of imperilment take effect, we analyze how they are applied in the narratives of the far right. In general, narratives are accounts that describe a situation or process in a way that makes certain goals and values seem to be a logical consequence.21 As such, narratives offer adequate access to the subject of interest, since they represent communicative actions designed to construct reality and to involve the recipients emotionally. In social science, the concept of narratives had long played a subordinate role but recently became more used after being popularized by civil society discourses.22 While there is no consensual definition of the term, it is convenient for our purpose to understand narratives as a Òcohesive and coherent account of events,Ó telling of actors whose actions Òresult in questions or conflicts for which answers or resolutions are provided.Ó23 However, with this definition (and other narrative approaches in social movement research as well), it is not clear how the concept of narratives differs from that of frames. This concept, in turn, can be understood as Òschemata of interpretationÓ that actors use to define a situation24 based on Òdiagnoses and prognosesÓ about reality that determine what is perceived as opportune action.25 Framing involves the selection of certain aspects of lifeÑthe perceived realityÑbound together in a narrative to Òdefine problems, specify causes, convey moral assessments, and endorse remedies.Ó26 The concept of frames thus presents semantics that are similar if not intersecting with the concept of narratives. However, to avoid entering a deeper debate on conceptual differences here,27 it suffices to note that the tools of frame analysis should be transferable to the analysis of narratives due to this semantic affinity."
text_normalised: Narratives are cohesive and coherent accounts of events that describe situations or processes in ways that make certain goals and values appear as logical consequences. They tell of actors whose actions result in questions or conflicts for which answers or resolutions are provided. Narratives represent communicative actions designed to construct reality and involve recipients emotionally. They function by selecting certain aspects of perceived reality and binding them together to define problems, specify causes, convey moral assessments, and endorse remedies. Through this selective presentation of events and their relationships, narratives shape how situations are understood and what actions appear appropriate or necessary in response to them.

text: "One approach to thinking about change in narrative interventions involves inserting prescriptive messages in an entertaining story. Prescriptive messages are often delivered through role models who portray desirable and undesirable behaviors (Bandura, 1986). The narra- tive format can be effective because it reduces resis- tance to persuasive attempts (Murrar & Brauer, 2019). Narrative media interventions using prescriptive mes- sages and role models to promote intergroup reconcili- ation (Paluck, 2009), address corruption (Blair et al., 2019), and counter gender-based violence (Green et al., 2020) have been shown to shift behaviors and per- ceived social norms but not personal beliefs. However, under some conditions (e.g., ongoing violence), pre- scriptive messages might be ineffective or backfire, for instance, if prescribed behaviors are risky, if the com- munity disapproves of the behaviors, or if community discussions counter the messages (e.g., Bilali et al., 2017; Paluck, 2010). This presents a challenge for inter- ventions tackling violent extremism because behaviors to prevent terrorist acts can be risky. A different approach to narrative interventions is to raise awareness and create scripts that broadly influ- ence peopleÕs worldviews (Petraglia, 2007). Narrative interventions use the power of storytelling to help people make meaning of their reality in a new way or help them imagine a different reality (Bruner, 1990; Greitemeyer, 2011) through encouraging reflection and engagement with different perspectives (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2013). Fictional narratives can simulate real- world experience, providing the opportunity to explore difficult situations, such as war, without the associated risk and trauma (Mar & Oatley, 2008). This approach can be suitable in violent-extremism contexts because it provides different scripts to understand reality with- out creating the ethical concerns of prescribing risky behaviors. However, it is not known whether such awareness-raising narratives can influence attitudes and behaviors."
text_normalised: A narrative is a story format that can convey messages and influence audiences through entertainment. Narratives may incorporate prescriptive messages delivered via role models who demonstrate desirable or undesirable behaviors, or they may function to raise awareness and provide alternative scripts for understanding reality. The narrative format operates by reducing resistance to persuasive content and enabling audiences to make meaning of their reality in new ways or imagine different realities. Narratives can simulate real-world experiences, allowing exploration of difficult situations without associated risks. Through storytelling, narratives encourage reflection and engagement with different perspectives, potentially influencing worldviews, attitudes, behaviors, and perceived social norms. The effectiveness of narratives depends on contextual conditions and the approach employed.

text: Conspiracy theories are a form of Narrative, defined as a shared belief system providing an alternative ideological framework to explain a situation and offer guidance as to how to behave to regain significance, control, and affiliations  (page 2)
text_normalised: A narrative is a shared belief system that provides an alternative ideological framework for explaining situations and offering guidance on how to behave in order to regain significance, control, and social affiliations. Narratives function as collective sense-making structures that interpret events or circumstances while simultaneously prescribing courses of action. They serve to restore or establish individuals' sense of meaning, agency, and connection to groups when these psychological needs are threatened or diminished. By offering both explanatory and prescriptive dimensions, narratives enable adherents to understand their circumstances through a particular ideological lens and to identify appropriate responses that address their needs for personal significance, perceived control over outcomes, and belonging to social collectives.

text: "Attempting to explain how people understand conflict in general, and intractable conflict in par- ticular, Bar-Tal (1998, 2007) introduced the idea of the ethos of conflict. He argued that people in societies embroiled in intractable conflict cope with the conflict by developing socially shared beliefs about it. The ethos of conflict, therefore, constitutes a socially shared belief system, com- prised of eight interrelated themes and beliefs, such as justness of oneÕs groupÕs goals, concern about security for oneÕs group, the special victimi- zation of oneÕs group, among others. Importantly, this socially shared belief system usually leads to the emergence of a dominant (or master) narra- tive of the conflict, endorsed by the majority of society (Bar-Tal, 1998; Hammack, 2006). Previous research found that endorsement of the ethos of conflict has consequences for conflict and peace, for example, reducing support for compromise and peaceful conflict resolution (Canetti et al., 2017). The idea of an ethos of conflict has thus been an important starting point in understanding how people frame intractable conflict, and how this understanding shapes the course of the conflict."
text_normalised: Narratives are socially shared belief systems that emerge from and organize collective understandings of significant social phenomena. They constitute coherent frameworks comprised of interrelated themes and beliefs that are endorsed by a majority within a society or group. Narratives function to help collectives make sense of complex situations by providing dominant interpretive structures. These belief systems are socially constructed and widely shared, representing collective rather than individual sense-making. Narratives shape how groups frame and understand their circumstances, and consequently influence attitudes and behaviors related to those circumstances. They serve as master frameworks that organize multiple thematic elements into a unified interpretive system that guides collective understanding and response.

text: Narratives refer to the ideological component of radicalization. From a psychological point of view, these narratives are useful for people because they establish what is considered valid to achieve personal significance (Webber & Kruglanski, 2017). Thus, people articulate their sense of reality around shared stories that give them meaning and certainty (page 51)
text_normalised: Narratives constitute ideological frameworks that establish criteria for what is considered valid in achieving personal significance. From a psychological perspective, they function as shared stories around which individuals articulate their sense of reality, providing meaning and certainty. These narratives serve as organizing structures that help people understand their experiences and determine legitimate pathways for fulfilling psychological needs related to significance and purpose.

text: radical ideologies (narrative) p. 52  radical narratives (i.e., legitimization of terrorism). (abstract)  The radical narrative was conceptualized as the legitimation of terrorist acts and it was evaluated with a single item (i.e., ÒThe 3/11 terrorist attacks in Madrid were fair and deservedÓ). Responses were measured on five_point Likert scale ranging from 1 (fully disagree) to 5 (fully agree). p.53
text_normalised: A narrative is a discursive construction that provides legitimation for particular actions or events. It functions as a framework through which actors justify or rationalize conduct that might otherwise be contested or condemned. Narratives operate by establishing evaluative positions regarding the fairness, deservedness, or appropriateness of specific acts, thereby shaping how those acts are interpreted and assessed. In this capacity, narratives serve as vehicles for expressing and communicating ideological stances, translating abstract beliefs into concrete judgments about particular occurrences. The narrative framework enables individuals to articulate positions on controversial or extreme actions by embedding them within broader systems of meaning and justification. Through this legitimating function, narratives bridge ideological commitments and evaluations of specific events or behaviors, providing coherent rationales that align actions with underlying belief systems.

text: The review builds on a social psychological framework that identifies important existential and epistemic needs that motivate individuals to become ideological extremists and discusses the mechanisms through which ideological narratives that promote political violence can serve these needs (page 107)  Thus, to resonate with a promotion focus, ideologies could emphasize the glory that violence against the enemies of oneÕs group provides, and the realistic expectation that oneÕs political goals are achievable through violence [21,22]. In other words, narratives can promise some form of special statusÑfor example, heroism, notoriety, martyrdomÑto violent perpetrators. This includes narratives that promote specific forms of violence (i.e. gun violence) as a means of attaining personal empowerment (Page 108)
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that serves existential and epistemic needs by providing ideological content capable of motivating action. Narratives function through mechanisms that resonate with individuals' psychological orientations, offering frameworks that connect means to ends. They can promise forms of status or empowerment to those who adopt particular courses of action, thereby making specific behaviors appear meaningful or achievable. Narratives operate by emphasizing potential outcomes and establishing expectations about what can be accomplished through certain means, thus serving to align ideological content with individual motivational states. They provide accounts that can promote particular forms of action as pathways to fulfilling psychological needs or achieving desired states.

text: The means to achieve significance are found in the collective narrative (ideology) of the ingroup, because the beliefs of the group inform what it means to be significant or essential in the eyes of others. If such a narrative identifies violence and terrorism as a means to achieve significance, people can support and commit to violence and terrorism. (page 399)
text_normalised: A narrative is a collective ideological framework held by an ingroup that defines the means through which members can achieve significance or essentiality in the eyes of others. It consists of shared beliefs that inform what constitutes meaningful action and prescribes pathways for attaining valued status within the group. The narrative establishes criteria for significance and identifies specific means—which may include particular forms of action or behavior—as legitimate or necessary routes to achieving this significance. By providing this interpretive framework, the narrative shapes members' understanding of how to fulfill valued roles and gain recognition according to the group's standards and values.

text: During the third debate leading up to the 2016 U.S. presidential election, a Muslim American asked the candidates how they would respond to rising Islamophobia. The candidates began their responses by opposing prejudice and then converged on a longstanding narrative that understands Muslims as a group with distinct responsibility for thwarting violence (page 1)  Both responses opposed anti-Muslim prejudice and in so doing also reinforced a central message to the Muslim questioner and to the broader audience: a minority of Muslims in America can potentially harm, and a peaceful majority has a responsibility to stop it (page 1, 2)
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that conveys particular understandings about social groups and their responsibilities or characteristics. Narratives can simultaneously express opposition to prejudice while reinforcing specific messages about group identities and obligations. They function as frameworks through which audiences interpret the roles, potential behaviors, and duties of particular social categories. Narratives may attribute distinct responsibilities to groups, positioning them in relation to potential threats or harms, and can communicate layered messages that shape how majorities and minorities are understood within a society. Through their structure and content, narratives convey central messages to both specific audiences and broader publics about group characteristics and expectations.

text: "Beyond flagging and taking down ISISÕ online content, counterterrorism strategies have relied primarily on reducing the appeal of ISISÕ ideology using counter-narratives, defined as an Òintentional and direct communication strategy, within a political, policy, or military context, to discredit messaging of a violent extremist natureÓ (Ferguson, 2016, p. 8). In a race to win the battle of Òthe hearts and the minds,Ó a slew of social media campaigns attempt to critique ISISÕs legitimacy on moral and religious grounds. Some are state-sponsored messages (e.g., United States State Department ÒRunÑdo not walk to ISIS landÓ); others include appeals from religious clerics or ISIS defectors as they are both perceived to be credible voices to challenge ISISÕ narrative."
text_normalised: Counter-narratives constitute intentional and direct communication strategies deployed within political, policy, or military contexts to discredit messaging of a violent extremist nature. These strategic communications aim to challenge the legitimacy of extremist messaging on moral, religious, or other grounds. Counter-narratives may originate from state-sponsored sources or from actors perceived as credible voices, such as religious authorities or former adherents of the targeted movement. The approach reflects an effort to contest ideological appeal through deliberate communicative intervention rather than content removal alone.

text: A popular explanation for the emergence of right-wing populism is that perceived threats toward migrants triggered a wave of anti-migrant sentiment. This kind of insecurity narrative paints ethnocentrism as a reaction to ongoing events rather than an entrenched belief that coexists with related right-wing ideologies. (page 337)
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that frames events or phenomena in terms of causal relationships, presenting them as reactions to or consequences of specific circumstances rather than as pre-existing conditions. Narratives function as explanatory frameworks that interpret social or political developments by establishing temporal and causal connections between events and responses. They construct particular understandings of reality by positioning beliefs, attitudes, or behaviors as outcomes of identifiable triggers or ongoing situations, thereby shaping how phenomena are perceived and understood. Through this framing, narratives distinguish between reactive responses and enduring dispositions, offering interpretive schemas that organize information about social processes and their origins.

text: "The early stage of Dialogical Self Theory was determined by personality psychology. With constructivist psychology, it stressed the discursive nature of the self and positioning, but mini- mized the social dimension of self-narratives (Fairclough, 1992, pp. 25, 64). Contemporary advocates of Dialogical Self Theory are more aware of the fact that self-narratives are consti- tuted by and constitute societal structures (Hermans, 2018, pp. 4, 139). This brought me to Critical Discourse Analysis as a research method, to study dialogical self in relation to society. In my view, Dialogical Self Theory and critical discourse analysis are compatible and complementary. Critical Discourse analysts use more or less the same key concepts as Dialogical Self theorists:  ÒSelfÓ: Critical discourse analysts speak about the self primarily in terms of subject positions or social identities (Fairclough, 1992, pp. 137Ð168). People do not ÔhaveÕ a self but are constituted and constitute themselves through discourses.  ÒPositionÓ: Critical discourse analysts assume that subjects are positioned and pos- ition themselves in social relationships (Fairclough, 1992, pp. 8, 64Ð65). Discourse is not only about positioning, but also about being positioned.  ÒVoiceÓ: Critical discourse analysts speak about voices in terms of inter-textuality and discourses (Fairclough, 1992, p. 105), these are the shared languages that (groups of) people use to construct (a vision of) social reality that is considered to be real and right.  ÒPolyphonyÓ: Critical discourse analysts speak about polyphony or multi-voicedness in terms of inter-discursivity or orders of discourse in the sense that discourses co-exist and compete to become dominant or peripheral (Fairclough, 1992, pp. 46-48).  ÒDialogueÓ: Critical discourse analysts speak about subjects constituting themselves and being constituted through dialogical intertextuality in terms of hegemony and hegemonic struggles (Fairclough, 1992, pp. 92, 103)."
text_normalised: Self-narratives are discursive constructions through which individuals constitute themselves and are constituted as subjects. These narratives are not merely personal accounts but are fundamentally shaped by and simultaneously shape societal structures and discourses. Self-narratives involve positioning, whereby individuals occupy and are assigned subject positions or social identities within social relationships through discourse. They incorporate voices understood as shared languages and discourses that groups employ to construct visions of social reality deemed legitimate. Self-narratives exhibit polyphony or multi-voicedness, reflecting the coexistence and competition of multiple discourses that may become dominant or peripheral. Through dialogical intertextuality, self-narratives participate in ongoing processes of meaning-making and social constitution, involving relations of power and hegemonic struggles. Rather than possessing fixed selves, individuals are continuously constituted through these narrative and discursive practices embedded in broader social contexts.

text: This article explores radicalization and deradicalization by considering the experiences of six young Tunisian people who had become Salafist Muslims. Their responses to narrative interviews and repertory grid technique are considered from a personal construct perspective, revealing processes of construing and reconstruing, as well as relevant aspects of the structure and content of their construct systems. (page 58)
text_normalised: Narratives are accounts or stories elicited through interview techniques that reveal individuals' processes of construing and reconstruing their experiences. These accounts provide access to the structure and content of personal construct systems, showing how individuals organize and interpret their social and psychological worlds. Through narrative forms, researchers can examine how people make sense of their experiences, including processes of meaning-making and cognitive reorganization. Narratives thus serve as methodological tools for understanding the frameworks through which individuals perceive and structure their reality, offering insight into both the content of their beliefs and the underlying cognitive architecture that shapes their interpretations.

text: " Past research on meaning in life highlights the importance of meaning frameworks that provide individuals with a sense of confidence and understanding of their reality. More importantly, meaning frameworks not only describe how the world generally operates, but also define worthy goals to pursue. Through com- mitment to those goals, an individual affirms her identity and asserts that her life matters (George & Park, 2016; Steele, 1988). In the context of political extremism, an ideological narrative fulfills this function by describing a collective cause that can earn an individual the significance they desire, as well as an appropriate means with which to pursue that cause. For example, an ideology may present violence as a way to bring the individual reverence, honor, and appreciation from the group (Kruglanski et al., 2013). An individual who subscribes to a violence-promoting narrative will be more likely to engage in violent extremism, because the narrative justifies violence as an effective way to attain signifi- cance, and presents it as moral and acceptable. Thus, under a heightened need for significance, an individual may be particularly sensitive to meaning frameworks that are explicit about significance-affording causes and directly promise a sense of mat- tering and purpose to those who subscribe to them. Because significance is defined uniquely in different cultures, ways of attaining it are spelled out in a cultural narrative that conditions significance on upholding and defending the groupÕs unique values. At times of peace and relative tranquility, such values typically consist of peaceful contributions to society, through service and facilitation of the groupÕs development and accomplishment of its objectives. A narrative espousing these values could state that the way to become significant and appre- ciated is through hard work, pursuit of a career, and/or Ògood worksÓ that benefit others. At times of intergroup feud, when the group perceives itself to be threatened by an enemy, however, a narrative may proclaim violence against the enemy as conferring supreme glory on the individual and bestowing on her or him the status of hero or martyr. Such a narrative warrants and legitimizes violent extremism as a supreme means to significance. In short, the role of the narrative is to pinpoint a preferred course of action from among several possible options and to legitimize that course as the best method for addressing an individualÕs aroused need for sig- nificance."

The narrative justifies specific actions as effective ways to attain significance and presents them as moral and acceptable. Cultural narratives condition significance on upholding and defending the group's unique values, spelling out culturally specific ways of attaining significance. The narrative's role is to pinpoint a preferred course of action from among several possible options and to legitimize that course as the best method for addressing an individual's need for significance.

text: Past research on meaning in life highlights the importance of meaning frameworks that provide individuals with a sense of confidence and understanding of their reality. More importantly, meaning frameworks not only describe how the world generally operates, but also define worthy goals to pursue. Through commitment to those goals, an individual affirms her identity and asserts that her life matters (George & Park, 2016; Steele, 1988). In the context of political extremism, an ideological narrative fulfills this function by describing a collective cause that can earn an individual the significance they desire, as well as an appropriate means with which to pursue that cause. For example, an ideology may present violence as a way to bring the individual reverence, honor, and appreciation from the group (Kruglanski et al., 2013). An individual who subscribes to a violence-promoting narrative will be more likely to engage in violent extremism, because the narrative justifies violence as an effective way to attain significance, and presents it as moral and acceptable. Thus, under a heightened need for significance, an individual may be particularly sensitive to meaning frameworks that are explicit about significance-affording causes and directly promise a sense of mattering and purpose to those who subscribe to them. Because significance is defined uniquely in different cultures, ways of attaining it are spelled out in a cultural narrative that conditions significance on upholding and defending the groupÕs unique values. At times of peace and relative tranquility, such values typically consist of peaceful contributions to society, through service and facilitation of the groupÕs development and accomplishment of its objectives. A narrative espousing these values could state that the way to become significant and appreciated is through hard work, pursuit of a career, and/or Ògood worksÓ that benefit others. At times of intergroup feud, when the group perceives itself to be threatened by an enemy, however, a narrative may proclaim violence against the enemy as conferring supreme glory on the individual and bestowing on her or him the status of hero or martyr. Such a narrative warrants and legitimizes violent extremism as a supreme means to significance. In short, the role of the narrative is to pinpoint a preferred course of action from among several possible options and to legitimize that course as the best method for addressing an individualÕs aroused need for significance. p. 109  Other social psychological research offers insight into potential reasons that extreme networks may have this influence. First, the presence of radicalized others may create a local norm that leads to a shared reality (Hardin & Higgins, 1996), that is, a consensually supported narrative wherein certain acts of violence are viewed as legitimate and appropriate. When this happens, the guilt and distress usually induced after transgressing against moral guidelines are reduced, as the violent act in question is no longer perceived as immoral (Webber, Schimel, Martens, Hayes, & Faucher, 2013). Rhetorical interactions within a group may augment the perceived importance of the groupÕs core purpose or its sacred values that justify the use of extreme means, including violence. Finally, the groupÕs continued existence may become an end in itself that motivates people to engage in extreme behavior for its sake (e.g., Gomez et al., 2011; Swann, Gmez, Dovidio, Hart, & Jetten, 2010). In other words, the groupÕs shared reality or consensually supported narrative affirms the groupÕs values; this makes salient activities that support those values and lends significance to members who carry them out. p.113  Narratives. According to the present theory, networks exert their influence via narratives; specifically, they make their narratives accessible to individuals and they validate them. It is the narratives, in turn, that ultimately serve as the platforms for actions. Thus, the greater oneÕs exposure to narratives that justify acts of violence, the greater the likelihood that individuals will become personally involved in violence. Narratives often serve as a bridge that connects feelings of insignificance and injustice to violent forms of remediation. For instance, analyses of rap lyrics have found that they provide listeners with justification for the use of violence (Kubrin, 2005). Similarly, analyses of Islamic poetry, often featured in propaganda magazines published by ISIS (Dabiq) and al Qaeda (Inspire), highlight their role in mobilizing support for violent jihad (Kendall, 2015). In our research on the extreme right in Germany, White power music was often the entry point into White nationalist and White supremacist ideology (Kruglanski, Webber, & Koehler, 2018). The music is forbidden by society and condenses and simplifies ideological tenets into catchy refrains that can be digested by youth. One interviewee described this music as the Òmain gateway drug into radical right-wing ideology.Ó Other narratives that link injustice to violence are conveyed by social norms that reward (or condone) violence, when employed for the goal of significance. This is true, for instance, of norms prevalent in the southern United States that perpetuate culture-of-honor mores (Cohen & Nisbett, 1997). Thus, Southerners are not generally more violent but do express greater violence in reaction to attacks on their personal honor that promote significance loss in the Southern culture (Cohen & Nisbett, 1994). Relatedly, men who were exposed to pornographic films depicting violence against women became more aggressive toward a woman who had insulted them (Donnerstein, Linz, & Penrod, 1987). The latter finding is in line with the notion that threats to significance are especially likely to elicit extreme reactions when the salient narrative justifies themÑin this case, by means of exposure to violent behavioral scripts in media. Generally, under heightened desire for meaning and significance, narratives that are accessible and endorsed by oneÕs social networks become more attractive. For instance, American participants who were experimentally induced to feel insignificant (via cued recall of a time they felt humiliated) were more extreme in their political beliefs than their counterparts who we not exposed to the manipulation (Webber et al., 2017). Relevant in this regard is empirical evidence gathered within terror management theory, which highlights the importance of culturally shared worldviews in restoring meaning and significance that was threatened by the awareness of mortality (Greenberg, Pyszczynski, & Solomon, 1986; Pyszczynski, Solomon, & Greenberg, 2015). For instance, researchers found that Iranian college students induced to experience a state of insignificance (via a mortality reminder) were more supportive of martyrdom attacks against the United States than individuals who did not experience such a reminder (Pyszczynski et al., 2006). pp. 113-114  Ideological disillusionment. There is evidence that extremists often leave radical movements because they become disillusioned with the ideological narrative, specifically with the aspects of it that deal with moral warrants for violence (e.g., Kruglanski, Webber, & Koehler, 2018; Reinares, 2011). Such conflict with alternative values reduces the significance conferring power of the violence justifying narrative. Neumann (2015), for instance, found that fighters often left ISIS because they struggled with the moral justification behind ISISÕ decision to engage in violence against other Muslims. Similarly, in a sample that varied across the ideological spectrum, Altier and colleagues (2017) found that 60% of extremists became disillusioned with the strategy or means by which their group sought political change, specifically with its moral warrant or its effectiveness, both reducing it perceived significance affording potential. p. 115

They serve as platforms for action by making certain behaviors accessible and validated within social networks. Narratives can create shared realities wherein specific acts are viewed as legitimate and appropriate, reducing moral distress by reframing actions as acceptable. They connect feelings and perceived injustices to forms of remediation by providing justification for particular behaviors. Under heightened desires for meaning, narratives that are accessible and endorsed by one's social networks become more attractive, as they offer significance-affording causes and promise a sense of mattering and purpose to those who subscribe to them.

text: "In everyday life, humans construct rich narratives that represent causal connections between different events and so imbue these connections with meaning or pur- pose. Indeed, one of the ways in which humans under- stand themselves is by generating autobiographical stories, or narrative identities, that represent the self in past, present, and imagined future contexts (McAdams, 2013). Coherent self-identities emerge gradually through adulthood from the integration of such narratives, which may themselves change over time, with social roles, psy- chological dispositions, motivations, and values (McAdams & McLean, 2013). With the right psychological ingredients in place, narratives can make bad ideas appear attractive and good ideas wholly unappealing. Of particular relevance to the study of radicalization are victimization narratives, or narratives that frame individuals or social groups as the victims of intentional harm(s) (Pemberton & Aarten, 2017). Attempts to under- stand experiences of victimization, to assign these experi- ences meaning, and to reconcile these experiences with oneÕs pre-existing identity may lead to the emergence of new narrative identities (Crossley, 2000). In Palestinian and Dutch Muslim youths, for example, perceiving oneself or oneÕs group as the victim of injustices was associated with greater support for violence and radicalism (Doosje, Loseman, & van den Bos, 2013; Victoroff et al., 2011). It is thus not surprising that propaganda materials produced and distributed by violent extremist organizations in an effort to garner support and to mobilize recruits routinely employ such victimization narratives. They are a powerful means for transmitting emotions and values."
text_normalised: Narratives are structured representations that establish causal connections between events, thereby imbuing these connections with meaning or purpose. They serve as frameworks through which individuals understand themselves and their experiences, integrating past, present, and imagined future contexts with social roles, psychological dispositions, motivations, and values. Narratives can shape the perceived attractiveness or appeal of ideas by framing events and experiences in particular ways. They function as means for assigning meaning to experiences and reconciling them with pre-existing identities, potentially leading to the emergence of new self-understandings. Narratives can frame individuals or social groups in specific relational positions, such as victims of intentional harms, and serve as vehicles for transmitting emotions and values between individuals or groups.

text: "Having discussed the necessity, but difficulty, of studying victimological processes in (de-)radi- calization, the next step is to understand how victimization works in deradicalization from political violence. In this issue, Pemberton and Aarten posited narrative as a metaphor for the study of victimization in political violence. They argue that since victimization is best under- stood through narrative19 and narrative is a root metaphor for studying radicalization,20 narra- tive seems the best route to studying victimization in radicalization and deradicalization. The narrative framework was discussed in detail in that article and will therefore not be repeated in detail in this article. In summary, narrative is an account of events in the order in which they occurred to make a point.21 However, not any event will do. A narrative begins with a particular event and this event Òis out of the ordinary, representing a deviation from the typical or routine aspects of the individualÕs lifeÓ22 or what Burke refers to as Òintentional trouble.Ó23 The notion that intentional trouble is involved in getting the narrative ball rolling can be connected to the victimization experience: the experience of suffering intentional harm. Previous research has shown that narratives of victimization can play a key role as nadir experiences and turning points in the stories that radicals and terrorists construct about their own lives and that of the group to which they belong.24 Either at the individual level or the group level a sense of past victimization can provide a powerful moral motive for subsequent acts of violence and aggression.25"

This initiating event involves the experience of suffering intentional harm. text: "The understanding that narrative concerns an Agent, performing an Action to achieve a Goal underlines BrunerÕs view that narratives are fundamentally about Òthe vicissitudes of human intention.Ó15 Events are not merely mentioned or described, but are causally con- nected, at least from the point of view of the protagonist. In stories, causality is shaped in terms of the intent of its characters. Bruner distinguishes the narrative mode of reasoning, which in his view people typically use to explain Òhow the human world worksÑhow and why, that is, human beings do what they do,Ó16 from the paradigmatic mode: the rational analysis, logical proof, and empirical observation that forms the basis for scientific reasoning. text: Narrative and Identity A key area of narrative research concerns narrative understanding of identity. Research in personality psychology gives credence to the view that life can be understood as narrative. McAdams23 argues that personality can best be seen as consisting of three levels. The first level, which McAdams terms the social actor, consists of traits, such as the well-known Big Five.24 Level II is termed the motivated agent and concerns personal strivings, life tasks, defense mechanisms, coping strategies, skills, and other motivational, developmental, or strategic constructs. What differentiates the agent from the actor is that the former is contextualized within time, place, and/or role. Whereas dispositional traits account for broad consistencies in how people behave across situation and over time, personal goals and motives address what people want (and fear) and how they strive to obtain what they want (and avoid what they fear) in particular social and developmental contexts and with respect to particular social roles.25 Level III involves identity narratives or self-stories, which McAdams calls the autobiographical author. This narrative identity draws on and is layered over traits and adaptations. Key is the understanding that Òbeyond dispositional traits and characteristic adaptations, human lives vary with respect to their integrative life stories or personal narratives that individuals construct to make meaning and identity in the modern world.Ó26 A narrative identity is an internalized, evolving, and integrated story of the self. It reconstructs the past, present, and future in such a way to provide a personÕs life with unity, purpose, and meaning. Through narrative identity, Òpeople convey to themselves and to others who they are now, how they came to be, and where they think their lives may be going in the future.Ó27 In other words, understanding the person is understanding his or her story. McAdams and McLean28 link the development of the three ways of understanding the selfÑthe social actor, the motivated agent, and the autobiographical authorÑto challenges associated with three different forms of selfawareness. The social actor is tasked with overcoming the challenge of self-regulation and the motivated agent with self-esteem. In addition to this the autobiographical author offers the self a means to integrate different experiences and episodes in life: through the coherent life story it constructs it provides the ÒIÓ with a continuous story of ÒmeÓ in space and time; in other words, it offers self-continuity. The self of today is the self of yesterday and the self of tomorrow. Any changes also have retrospective implications: events in the past are reinterpreted in the light of the current understanding of a life story. The drive to achieve self-continuity means that the self-attempts to bring the present in line with the past and vice versa. pp. 543-544  According to Burke,13 all stories have at least in common that they contain an Agent who performs an Action to achieve a Goal in a recognizable Setting by the use of certain Means. What drives the story is a mismatch between the elements of this ÒpentadÓ: what Burke refers to as ÒTrouble.Ó The story is one that is unexpected, and the plot and its resolution must be seen in conjecture with the efforts of the characters in the story to cope with, resolve, integrate, or overcome the unexpected event and its consequences.14 The understanding that narrative concerns an Agent, performing an Action to achieve a Goal underlines BrunerÕs view that narratives are fundamentally about Òthe vicissitudes of human intention.Ó15 Events are not merely mentioned or described, but are causally connected, at least from the point of view of the protagonist. In stories, causality is shaped in terms of the intent of its characters. Bruner distinguishes the narrative mode of reasoning, which in his view people typically use to explain Òhow the human world worksÑhow and why, that is, human beings do what they do,Ó16 from the paradigmatic mode: the rational analysis, logical proof, and empirical observation that forms the basis for scientific reasoning. The importance of intent in narratives lays bare the connection to ethics and morality: in narratives things happen for a reason, and this reason concerns either good or bad intentions. 17 Even if an event happened by chance, morality will still feature heavily in the narrative, with the characters querying the lack of intent, or reason behind the event that shapes their own further existence. Overall, the narrative imposes structure and sequences events in such a fashion it becomes a coherent plot and that an evaluation of these events becomes possible.18 As will be discussed later in this article, Ògetting a life,Ó that is, the construction of a coherent life story is one of the most important elements of an individualÕs personality development from adolescence onward.19 pp. 542-543  Even though Kruglanski and colleaguesÕ work does not refer to the body of literature discussed in the previous sections, this article argues that narrative psychology can be an added value to this theory. Two points need to be made. First, it seems that Kruglanski and colleagues view radicalization on the levels of the social actor and the motivational agent, but not on the level of the autobiographical author. Yet given the ideological component of radicalization and the coincidence of identity and ideology, narrative can offer a useful framework of perceiving the pathways to radicalization and political violence. As Haidt, Graham, and Joseph34 explain: ÒLevel III centrally concerns identity, and more specifically identity as experienced in a narrative mode. At this level, the stories people tell themselves and others about how they came to hold the moral and political beliefs they currently hold should be examined. These stories are not expected to be literally true as historical accounts, but it is expected that they influence a personÕs behavior, including political behavior such as voting, and involvement in political movements.Ó And, in particular to radical, extremist political activity, including terrorist acts, the authors would hazard to conjecture. The nonbehavioral components of radicalization can be understood along the dimensions of the extent of agreement with given causes and the extent to which the ideology forms a component of someoneÕs identity. The extent to which the master narrative of the terrorist organization coincides with the life narrative of an individual goes beyond mere attitudinal agreement: it forges an identity based union.35 A second point is that Kruglanski et al.Õs notion of significance quest appears, not only terminologically, to have a strong connection to the terroristÕs life narrative. Yet they view this term solely in terms of attitudinal constructs and as a goal to which the self as a motivational agent aspires. Yet it is believed that the significance quest is (also) an element of peopleÕs overarching life narrative. Like the choice for an occupation, a spouse or habitus, the choice for this quest says more about a person than merely a strong preference: it says something about who they are, also to themselves. Finally, the fact that the narrative rupture also applies to the connection with wider society also can provide insight in important mechanisms that underlie the connection of victimological processes to the significance quest.36 The experience of lost connection between oneÕs life story and the master narrative of society often leads to a view that only others with similar experiences can understand oneÕs experiences. Together with these peers those experiencing such a narrative rupture can engage in the co-construction of a smaller scale community narrative.37 In turn this community narrative can replace (parts of) the role of the cultural master narrative in the development of oneÕs identity, and form the basis for the significance quest.38 The narrative perspective thus provides both insights into the processes by which this occurs, but also offers the view that narrative through which radicalization occurs can be co-created by people living through the same victimization experiences. pp. 545-546  Narrative and Emotions As noted above, nuclear episodes are important components of a life story. They are critical events that are often described as turning points in an individualÕs life story. These events have the capacity to trigger (strong) emotion(s) and thus emotions form the nucleus of a narrative. The process model of Frijda39 views the trigger of emotion as an appraisal of a situation that is out of the ordinary. This appraisal is inherently evaluative: it relates probable outcomes of the unexpected event to the individualÕs concerns, thereby relating the event to the individuals past and future selves. The autobiographical experience of victimization can give rise to a whole host of emotions. Each of these emotions is associated with different action tendencies. The emotion in question guides the appraisal of the situation and subsequently leads to radically different actions. The most obvious ones are related to anger, which is the emotion associated with the experience of injustice, and can include vengefulness, hatred, but also forgiveness, contempt, and disgust.40 Narrative also transmits emotions.41 According to OatleyÕs taxonomy of emotional response to literary narratives there are assimilative and accommodative schema. The former concerns the empathic, interactional, and autobiographical responses noted above. Here, the narrator can draw on the emotions of the reader/ listener to get the story across. The story appeals to the readerÕs curiosity, where Òincompleteness can provoke arousal, and the reader becomes engaged in assimilating new elements to the schema until completion and relief occur.Ó42 A particular form of assimilative communication is covered by the concept of framing, in which a very brief narrative, often consisting of no more than a stereotypical image, can be used to transmit a compelling argument to a proven and potentially receptive audience.43 Framing relies on schemata shared by the communicator and the target of communication. The frame supplies the material to define problems and their causes, to clarify the moral issues involved and to point to suitable remedies. The most ambitious form of framing, so-called frame transformation, attempts to substantially alter the manner in which the target audience views a particular social or political issue.44 In doing so it relies on a novel connection between the particular issue at hand and a stock meta-frame, about which the target audience has already an established emotionally charged view. In accommodative schemas, the narrator has to overcome resistance, and/or (purposely) makes easy assimilation more difficult. Where assimilative schemas can rely on the listener agreeing with the narratorÕs point, and seeking to remember experiences, evidence and stories that confirm the narratorÕs position, accommodative schemas, make for a harder sell. The initial resistance will lead to a search for incongruities, counterarguments, and mistakes. 45 The former entails the target asking the question ÒCan I believe it?,Ó the latter ÒMust I believe it?Ó Within accommodative schemas it is worthwhile to distinguish between the elicitation of outright adverse emotions and of conflicting emotions. The latter is the case when communication elicits both positive, approach-oriented emotions and negative, avoidance- oriented emotions. As will be noted below, this conflict is an important feature of the reaction to victimological experience. Viewing victims can trigger sympathy and compassion, but also disgust, fear, and distress at the same time.46 Narrative is a key ingredient in shaping emotions experienced as a collective. In a recent review Bernard Rim_e emphasized the importance of sharing narrated emotions as a means to establish bonds within communities.47 Indeed, much of the fabric of groups, communities, and even nations and cultures consists in these bonds. Where collectives may experience emotional contagion when witnessing events or as a consequence of being in close proximity to others, the two other main paths to collective emotional experience rely on narrative.48 Key events in collective memory are accompanied by a narrativeÑoften supplied by a metaframe49Ñwhich gives rise to a shared appraisal of the event itself, its causes and consequences, its meaning and the emotions that are appropriate as a reaction to discussing this event. Narrative is also an agent in experiencing emotions as a member of a collective. Narrative connects personal experience to that of an encompassing cultural group (see below), and in addition signals whether or not a particular event should rightly be experienced as a collective issue. Evidence is accumulating that emotions that are experienced in such a Òwe-modeÓ have qualitatively different characteristics and associated action tendencies than emotions experienced in Òi-mode.Ó  Narrative and Culture The construction of culture is largely narrative in nature.68 Collective memories concern historical moments in a groupÕs existence, with narratives that institutionalize these memories into coherent stories.69 The memory is not only continued through time by storytelling and re-telling, but its narrative nature also emerges in the way collective memories are shaped and re-shaped by current-day needs. Instead of understanding the collective memories of the past as a fixed canon, they are re-interpreted in light of present events. These cultural narratives about national history, ethnicity, religion, and politics shape the personal stories people live by, and these personal stories can sustain or transform culture.70 In other words, the interaction between culture and identity works through narrative. For instance, Hammack71 defines identity as Òideology cognized through the individual engagement with discourse, made manifest in a personal narrative constructed and reconstructed across the life course and scripted in and through social interaction and social practice.Ó Cultural narratives not only provide a sense of self-continuity but also continuity with the other members of oneÕs community. As Hammack and Pilecki72 note, narrative provides the solution Ònot only to a need to see oneself as the same from one day to the next, but also to see oneself as engaged in a cognitive process that is the same as others within a particular time and place.Ó Culture provides a menu of stories to which the personÕs autobiographical narrative can relate.73 Culture provides (implicit) definitions of what is and what is not narrative, what is a good narrative, and the sites where telling narrativesÑor at least particular types of narrativeÑis or is not appropriate.74 But individuals can also find themselves struggling to square their own narrative with the master narrative in society, and in some fundamental way find themselves to be outsiders or deviants.75 This is also and particularly true for those who go through sudden, life-altering experiences that lead to Òshattered assumptionsÓ or Ònarrative ruptures.Ó76 The sense of alienation from the master narrative of society, and the need to connect to others who share similar experiences, goes a long way to explain the spontaneous emergence of self-help, mutual aid, and/ or more explicitly politically motivated groups who have a particular experience in common.77 Whether that is disease, addiction, or indeed victimization, this experience, the view that only others with this experience can fully comprehend what the individual is going through and in tandem the distance from the narratives the culture supplies, underlies this self-organization, and forms the point of departure for the construction of a group-based community narrative. The latter lies at the heart of sub- or countercultures.78 pp. 549-550
text_normalised: A narrative is an internalized, evolving story that reconstructs past, present, and future to provide unity, purpose, and meaning. It consists of an agent performing actions to achieve goals in recognizable settings through certain means, with events causally connected from the protagonist's perspective. Narratives are fundamentally concerned with human intention, distinguishing them from paradigmatic reasoning through their focus on why people do what they do. They impose structure and sequence events into coherent plots that enable evaluation. Narratives draw upon and integrate dispositional traits and characteristic adaptations, conveying who individuals are, how they came to be, and where their lives may be going. They provide self-continuity across time and space, with present understandings retrospectively reinterpreting past events. Narratives are shaped by and interact with cultural master narratives, which provide frameworks for personal stories while also potentially creating tensions when individual experiences diverge from culturally available storylines.

text: " The intergenerational effects of conflict can also be transmitted through narratives about conflict. Because many of the contemporary armed conflicts that exist today often pit national, ethnic, and religious groups against one another, identification and meaning making around these groups and their histories play an important role in how children and adolescents make sense of their social worlds (Barber, 2009; Hammack, 2010). Research suggests that as children age and become more aware of their surroundings and the messages their social world provides to them, they begin to con- struct their identities and attitudes based in part on the content of these messages (Merrilees et al., 2018; Nesdale, 2004). Within the context of political violence and armed conflict these messages include information about the history of their groupÕs suffering, the characteristics of and acts perpe- trated by out-group members, and broader messages about the legitimization of the use of violence in the name of group preservation." "That is, narratives can function as a tool for promoting psychological adjustment such as resilience and coping capability at the personal level but can also function to fuel negative intergroup attitudes and violence."
text_normalised: Narratives are accounts that convey information about a group's history, including experiences of suffering, characteristics and actions of out-group members, and broader messages regarding the legitimacy of violence for group preservation. These accounts serve as messages through which individuals, particularly as they develop awareness of their social environment, construct their identities and attitudes. Narratives function at multiple levels: at the personal level, they can promote psychological adjustment, resilience, and coping capability; at the intergroup level, they can fuel negative attitudes toward out-groups and legitimize violence. Through these accounts, individuals engage in meaning-making processes that shape how they understand their social worlds and their group's place within them.

text: ideological narrative that justifies political violence (abstract)  the present approach identifies three factors: individual motivation (needs), ideological justification of violence (narratives), and group processes (networks) (see also Ref. [21 _ ]). p. 131  Thus, in both the deviant movement toward extremism and the return to moderation, we see the interplay of a triumvirate of forces: the need to feel significant, the narrative that justifies political violence, and the network of social influence. p. 133
text_normalised: A narrative is an ideological framework that provides justification for particular forms of action or belief. In the context of political behavior, narratives function as cognitive structures that legitimize specific courses of conduct by offering rationales that align with broader ideological commitments. These narratives operate alongside individual psychological needs and social network influences to shape behavioral outcomes. A narrative serves as the interpretive lens through which individuals understand the appropriateness or necessity of their actions, embedding personal motivations within larger systems of meaning. The narrative component represents the ideological dimension of belief systems, distinguishing it from purely psychological drives or social pressures. Narratives thus constitute the justificatory discourse that bridges individual inclinations and collective norms, enabling actors to frame their choices as coherent with overarching principles or worldviews.

text: In reviewing the literature, we identify three factors critical to radicalization: (1) the individual need that motivates one to engage in political violence, (2) the ideological narrative that justifies political violence, and (3) the social network that influences oneÕs decisions along the pathway to extremism. (page 131)
text_normalised: A narrative is an ideological framework that provides justification for political violence. It serves as a legitimating structure that rationalizes engagement in violent action by offering moral, political, or philosophical grounds for such behavior. The narrative operates as one component within a broader process, working alongside individual motivations and social influences to shape decisions and actions. It functions to bridge personal needs and collective action by supplying a coherent rationale that transforms violence from a transgressive act into a justified or necessary response. The narrative's role is fundamentally justificatory, providing the interpretive lens through which individuals come to view political violence as acceptable, warranted, or obligatory within a particular ideological framework.

text: "Both he, and later Borchardt,20 emphasize that the cultural and reli- gious ingredients necessary for ÒDoomsday narrativesÓ (to quote the latter) are ever-present in society; notions of idealized pasts, cultural and moral purity, present evil, and spiritual retribution. However, only when the usual securitiesÑeconomic, social, religious, and political institutionsÑfail sectors of society can such narratives be mobilized to overtake the popular imagination." "Millenarian narratives can offer not only meaning, but hope, and a course of action. As Borchardt says, ÒDoomsday narrativesÓ are Òstrategies of persuasion,Ó36 and this means that someone is doing the persuading. What charismatic authority has the unique capacity for, to quote Andreas, is to allow a Ò... leader to mobilize people without the benefits or constraints of formal organization.Ó37 "Grand narratives contain overriding notions of purity, which justify violence as social cleansing. Accordingly, observance of the ÒrulesÓ in both groups is what maintains membersÕ Òpurity,Ó and therefore the purity of the group as a whole, engendering a collective responsi- bility to obey. As the apocalyptic stage is set (and strategically portrayed as impending in everyday life), the group leaders are dispensing the rules that they claim will make their side the winning one on Judgment Day. Compliance to their rules and continued obedience thus becomes a coping and control mechanism for group members, in daily life, and in the face of impending disaster."
text_normalised: Narratives are structured accounts that draw upon cultural and religious elements—such as idealized pasts, notions of purity, present evil, and spiritual retribution—which exist latently within society. They become mobilized and gain traction when conventional securities (economic, social, religious, and political institutions) fail, allowing these accounts to overtake popular imagination. Narratives function as strategies of persuasion, deployed by leaders to mobilize people without formal organizational structures. They contain overriding themes that can justify action, offer meaning and hope, and prescribe courses of conduct. By establishing rules and framing events as significant or impending, narratives create collective responsibility and serve as mechanisms for coping and control among adherents in daily life and in response to perceived crises.

text: "Research on terrorism and the Internet is characterized by a focus on examining how ter- rorists use the Internet for various purposes including fund-raising, recruitment, and indoc- trination by analyzing (both quantitatively and qualitatively) terrorist activity online and, as Sageman points out, open source datasets comprising communications and documents found on violent extremist websites. Much of the research applies methods of textual analy- sis to deconstruct the terrorist narrative in order to make recommendations for the construc- tion of counternarratives; to shed light on the motives and drivers of terrorist actors; or to provide some clues to the process of radicalization. While studies on the terrorist discourse are useful for developing an understanding of master narratives that terrorists use to influ- ence and motivate action, they tend to ignore a vital element in the communication pro- cessÑthe audienceÑwho receive, decode, internalize, and in some cases act on the messages embedded in these narratives. The audience plays a central role in media and communica- tion models. Yet analysis and empirical studies of terrorism tend to assume that the terrorist messages reach and influence a submissive audience primed for radicalizationÑoften by vir- tue of cursory traits such as demographics or religious belief. Where the literature does give some consideration to the audiences of violent extremist narrativesÑdefined here as those members of publics that terrorists seek to communicate with and influenceÑthe audience tends to be constructed into rudimentary and broad categories of government/ victim and supporters. A more comprehensive approach would also give consideration to the contexts, social situations, and extraneous factors that impact on the ways in which different individu- als and groups receive, construct, deconstruct, and reconstruct the terroristsÕ message as active consumers, and producers, of terrorist messaging."
text_normalised: Narratives are communicative constructs containing embedded messages that are used to influence and motivate action. They function as vehicles through which actors seek to communicate with and affect target audiences. Narratives are received, decoded, and internalized by audiences, who may subsequently act upon the messages they contain. Rather than being passively absorbed, narratives are actively engaged with by their recipients, who receive, construct, deconstruct, and reconstruct the messages as both consumers and producers. The effectiveness and meaning of narratives are shaped by the contexts, social situations, and extraneous factors that impact how different individuals and groups process them. Narratives thus operate within a communication process involving both message construction by senders and active interpretation by audiences, whose responses cannot be assumed to be uniform or submissive.

text: ÒIdentityÓ is understood here as that package of values, rooted in an historical narrative, strategically constructed in response to a sociohistorically specific reality.12 p. 359  For the purposes of this study, ÒradicalizationÓ is defined as the process by which an individual or collective increasingly adheres to a selectively literalist interpretation of an identity narrative (e.g., ideology), a response triggered and catalyzed by perceptions of crisis that may lead to the legitimization of and engagement in violence against perceived Others as a solution to those crises. p. 360  The core narrative in extremist propaganda tends to follow a broadly similar mantra: we are the epitome of the ingroup identity, the ingroupÕs crises are due to malevolent Others, so support us because we are your champions and protectors who will confront our enemies and restore the ingroupÕs glory with our political agenda. p. 360  The ingroup is thus increasingly perceived as the source of solutions typically due to it offering an explanatory narrative to makes sense of the world, a physical sanctuary via a collective of like minded individuals and a blueprint for tangible action rooted in both. pp. 360-361  Radical narratives variously interplay identity, crisis and solution constructs as a means to not only lure its audiences into perceiving the world through its competitive system of meaning but to catalyze CCR processes and drive radicalization. As graphically represented by vertical arrows in Figure 2, value-reinforcing messages tie the ingroup identity to solution constructs and Others to perceptions of crisis. This type of messaging is designed to reinforce the ingroupÕs positive values and actions and the OtherÕs negative values and actions. Dichotomy-reinforcing messaging, represented by horizontal arrows (Figure 2), tend to either accentuate the dichotomy between in- and outgroup attributes or demonstrate how solutions are required to address crises. By highlighting these dualities, dichotomy-reinforcing messages are used to both generate psychological, existential and sociopolitical anxieties in readers and provide readers with clear choices between the ingroup or Others and solution or crisis. Third, crisis-reinforcing messages typically tie treacherous ingroup members to ingroup crises. This type of messaging is particularly pertinent when analyzing Islamist propaganda because it reflects a groupÕs takfirist proclivities. Drawing on this range of narrative approaches is a means by which radical groups seek to strategically compel audiences to use identity-choice and/or rational-choice decision-making processes.25 Analyzing how Inspire and DabiqÕs contents prioritize value-, dichotomy-, and crisis-reinforcing narratives offers unique insights into not only how AQAP and IS want their readership to perceive the world but the types of decision-making processes its messaging seeks to trigger. pp. 361-362
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account rooted in historical content that functions as a framework for interpreting reality and constructing meaning. Narratives organize understanding by establishing relationships between identity constructs, perceived crises, and proposed solutions. They operate as explanatory systems that make sense of the world by defining ingroups and outgroups, attributing causality to events, and prescribing courses of action. Narratives are strategically constructed in response to specific sociohistorical contexts and can be selectively interpreted to varying degrees of literalism. They serve to reinforce values, accentuate dichotomies between groups, and generate or address anxieties by highlighting dualities and choices. Through interweaving identity, crisis, and solution elements, narratives function as competitive systems of meaning that shape audience perceptions and can catalyze decision-making processes, offering both cognitive frameworks for interpretation and blueprints for tangible action.

text: we define a narrative as any cohesive and coherent account of events with an identifiable beginning, middle, and end about characters engaged in actions that result in questions or conflicts for which answers or resolutions are provided. (page 383)
text_normalised: A narrative is a cohesive and coherent account of events that possesses an identifiable beginning, middle, and end. It centers on characters who engage in actions that generate questions or conflicts. The narrative structure provides answers or resolutions to these questions or conflicts. The account maintains internal consistency and logical connection among its elements, ensuring that the sequence of events forms a unified whole. This definition encompasses the essential structural components—temporal organization, character agency, problem generation, and resolution—that distinguish narratives from other forms of discourse or representation.

text: "There is no generally accepted definition of narrative. In many cases people treat story and narrative as synonyms. In narratology the former is an account of a related sequence of events, whereas the latter is the story as told, that is, by a particular storyteller in a particular context (see Abbott, 2008). My focus here will be on a narrative system, Òa coherent system of interrelated and sequentially organized stories that share a common rhetorical desire to resolve a conflict by establishing audience expectations according to known trajectories of its literary and rhetorical formÓ (Halverson, Goodall, and Corman, 2011:14). In the preceding definition, ÒtrajectoriesÓ refer to the narrative arc (see Figure 1). Stories, especially the ones told by extremists, are grounded in conflict (or some other kind of deficiency). The conflict creates a desire for a resolution. There may be an actual resolution if the story is an historical one, or projected into the future if the story is ongoing. The desire and resolution are connected by an arc of people, actions, and events that lead from one to the other."

There may be an actual resolution if the story is historical, or the resolution may be projected into the future if the story is ongoing. The desire and resolution are connected by an arc of people, actions, and events that lead from one to the other.
