text: Outlining the martyrdom rhetoric of Zawahiri can show the persuasive strategies used to recruit and radicalize, which opens up possible sites for dialogue and disruption. ZawahiriÕs speeches offer a glimpse into the motivations of extremists, because ideology is both in the mind and in discourse (Trethewey et al., 2009). Zawahiri renders a vision of the ideal martyr and, in doing so, creates an Òaspirational identityÓ that may resonate with those who follow him (Lederman & Menegatos, 2011) (page 7)
text_normalised: A narrative is a discursive construction that renders a vision of ideal identities and motivations, functioning as a persuasive strategy that may resonate with audiences. Narratives exist both cognitively and discursively, articulating ideological positions through rhetorical means. By outlining particular identities and values, narratives create aspirational models that can influence followers' self-conceptions and actions. The persuasive dimension of narratives operates through their capacity to align audience members with the ideals and motivations presented, thereby shaping identification and potential behavioral outcomes. Narratives thus serve as sites where ideology is both expressed and transmitted, offering insight into the belief systems of those who construct them while simultaneously working to recruit adherents to those systems.

text: The affordance factor includes five influences: (a) opportunity for immediate, concrete engagement with active ARR groups, (b) a consensual injustice narrative that condenses conspiracy-theory blame for system and self-dissatisfaction onto the outgroup, (c) narratives that convey heroic participation in a cosmic battle between good (own group) vs. evil (outgroup), (d) justifying narratives for religious aggression, and (e) unfalsifiable religious arguments. p. 7
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that condenses explanations for dissatisfaction or grievances by attributing blame to specific targets, conveys meaning through framing events as part of larger moral or cosmic struggles between opposing forces, and provides justification for particular courses of action. Narratives achieve consensus within groups by offering coherent interpretations of complex situations, organizing perceptions of injustice, heroism, and group identity. They function as cognitive and rhetorical tools that shape understanding of social reality, define in-group and out-group boundaries, and legitimate responses to perceived threats or wrongs. Through their capacity to simplify causality and assign moral valence, narratives influence collective sense-making and can motivate engagement with social movements or ideological positions.

text: "The complex interplay of identity, crisis, and solution constructs is crucial to under- standing the radicalization process. For the purposes of this study, ÒidentityÓ is defined as that package of values, rooted in an historical narrative, strategically constructed in response to a sociohistorically specific reality.12 According to this approach, ÒvaluesÓ are the fundamental building blocks of identity underscoring why identity constructs play such a significant cognitive role in shaping how individuals evaluate themselves, others and events. As Rokeach asserts, values act, Ò. . . as a standard or criterion for guiding action, for developing and maintaining attitudes toward relevant objects or situations, for justifying oneÕs own and otherÕs actions and attitudes, for morally judging self and others, and for comparing self with others.Ó13 Identity thus provides one of the fundamental cog- nitive prisms through which perceptions are shaped and actions justified. Echoing Hall,14 Martin,15 and Sen16 this definition acknowledges that identities are strategically con- structed in response to contextual factors."
text_normalised: A narrative is a historically rooted account that provides the foundation for constructing identity by packaging values in response to specific sociohistorical realities. Narratives supply the historical grounding from which values—the fundamental building blocks of identity—are derived and organized. These values function as standards or criteria that guide action, shape attitudes toward objects and situations, justify one's own and others' actions and attitudes, enable moral judgment of self and others, and facilitate social comparison. Through this process, narratives provide a fundamental cognitive framework through which individuals perceive and interpret themselves, others, and events. Narratives are strategically constructed in response to contextual factors, reflecting the sociohistorically specific circumstances in which they emerge and operate.

text: This article analyzes issues 1Ð5 of the Taliban in KhurasanÕs Azan magazine. It applies an interpretive framework for analyzing radical narratives, based on a multidisciplinary conceptualization of the radicalization process, to explore how Azan attempts to appeal to its audiences by leveraging ingroup, Other, crisis and solution constructs via value-, crisis-, and dichotomy-reinforcing narratives. (page 560)
text_normalised: Narratives are communicative constructs that leverage specific thematic elements—including ingroup identity, representations of the Other, crisis framing, and proposed solutions—to appeal to audiences. They function through reinforcing mechanisms that emphasize values, crises, and dichotomies. In the context of persuasive communication, narratives operate by articulating group boundaries, characterizing external entities, identifying perceived threats or problems, and presenting resolutions. These constructs work together to create coherent frameworks that can influence audience interpretation and response. Narratives thus serve as structured means of organizing and presenting information that connects identity, opposition, urgency, and action in ways designed to resonate with target audiences.

text: "The mechanisms of moral disengagement through which individuals justify violence, dehumanize victims, disregard the harmful consequences of violence and absolve themselves of blame have been used in the construction of violent extremist narratives." " The majority of research on moral disengagement in the field of terrorism studies examines extremist narratives in relation to the mechanisms of moral disengagement. A study by Hafez of the last will and testament video speeches made by Palestinian suicide bombers drew linkages between the content of these media products and mechanisms of moral disengagement. In HafezÕs study Palestinian suicide bombers used moral justification and dehuminization to moralize their violence as serving an altruistic cause of freedom from an oppressive and dangerous threat.24 AlyÕs analysis of the narratives employed on Islamist extremist websites acknowledges that biographical narratives of suicide bombers on such websites adhere to a strict format that portray the suicide bomber as a devout martyr mo- tivated to self-sacrifice by absolute submission to faith and an intense desire to fulfill the greatest demonstration of piety possible. Extremist narratives also displace the responsibil- ity for violence on the victims of terrorist acts claiming that atrocities perpetrated against Muslims by Western regimes are the primary cause for their retaliatory actions.25 The claims made in extremist narratives empower individuals to absolve themselves of blame for inhumane acts and behaviors while religion provides a moral template for justifying acts of violence as a moral response to perceived injustice."
text_normalised: Narratives are structured accounts or stories that convey particular interpretations of events, actors, and moral frameworks. They function as vehicles through which individuals or groups articulate justifications for actions, assign responsibility, characterize others, and construct moral meaning around behaviors and their consequences. Narratives organize information according to specific formats or templates that shape how events are portrayed and understood. They serve to legitimize conduct by framing it within broader moral, ideological, or causal schemas, enabling actors to position themselves and others in relation to perceived threats, injustices, or obligations. Through their content and structure, narratives provide frameworks for interpreting reality that can support particular courses of action by establishing moral boundaries, attributing causation, and defining the nature of relationships between groups or individuals.

text: "The narrative life-story method, proposed by McAdams (2001), is based on the assumption that narrating a life story is a normal human activity and through the narrative accounts people reveal who they are, who they want to be and provide justification, meaning, and efficacy to their lives."
text_normalised: A narrative is an account through which individuals reveal their identity, aspirations, and provide justification, meaning, and efficacy to their lives. The construction of such accounts constitutes a normal human activity whereby people articulate who they are and who they want to become. Through narrative, individuals engage in sense-making processes that establish coherence and purpose in their experiences. Narratives serve as vehicles for self-presentation and self-understanding, enabling people to communicate their sense of self while simultaneously constructing and maintaining that sense of self through the act of narration itself.

text: We propose that Islamist communications focus on eliciting change in emotional states, specifically inducing the paratelic-excitement mode, by focusing around a meta-narrative of Muslims as a unitary grouping self-defined as victim to Western aggression. Early indicators are that some genres of Islamist propaganda may be more effective than others in generating these emotional change states (e.g. cartoons) and some groupings appear to be more susceptible than others. (page 2)
text_normalised: A narrative is a communicative structure that focuses on a meta-level account of a defined group and its relationship to external forces. It functions to elicit changes in emotional states among audiences by presenting the group through particular framings, such as victim-aggressor dynamics. Narratives operate by establishing a unitary group identity and positioning that group within a broader relational context. They serve as vehicles for emotional influence, with effectiveness varying across different communicative genres and audience susceptibilities. The narrative framework organizes information to shape how group members understand their collective position and experiences in relation to others.

text: "Propaganda, then, is the deliberate attempt to persuade the public, through the commu- nication of narrative, that your particular idea is right. It differs from normal communication only inasmuch as the propagandist takes special care to craft her or his narrative to sway opinion, rather than to objectively present fact. Facts are important, but perception and memory are more so." "In the decade since he rose to prominence by declaring war on the ZionistÐCrusader alliance led by the United States, Osama bin Laden has had ample opportunity to set out the Al Qaeda narrative. The simplicity and coherence of that story has become increasingly important as the Al Qaeda movement has shifted from being a centralized group with stable senior membership to being effectively a brand that can appropriate any act of jihadi terror by groups and individuals around the world. Al QaedaÕs ideological narrative has at its heart the desire for a return to Islamic purity, and the division of the world into two distinct groupings, an ÒusÓ and a Òthem.Ó On the ÒusÓ side of the equation are a vanguard of virtuous Muslims, conscious of the true Islam. The ÒthemÓ is an unholy alliance of CrusaderÐZionists, with a centuries-long record of scheming to do down Islam, allied with the corrupt and degenerate political leadership of the Muslim world, who are thwarting the desire of Muslims to return to their true faith. Here then is a Manichean struggle between good and evil; civilizational in dimension and utopian in aspiration."
text_normalised: Narrative is a deliberately crafted communication designed to persuade an audience by shaping perception and memory rather than objectively presenting facts. It functions as a coherent story that organizes information to sway opinion toward a particular idea or worldview. A narrative typically establishes clear boundaries between groups, often through binary distinctions, and provides a framework for interpreting events and identities. It can serve as an ideological tool that unifies disparate actors under a shared understanding, functioning effectively as a recognizable brand or template that others can adopt. The narrative's persuasive power derives from its simplicity and coherence, which enable it to structure collective meaning and guide interpretation of complex realities. While facts may be incorporated, the narrative's primary function is to construct a particular version of reality that advances specific goals or perspectives.

text: "This may reveal something important about militant-extremist movements. Although militant-extremist leaders no doubt play a key role, it is probably not necessary for participants in mili- tant-extremist movements to be brainwashed or severely in- doctrinated. All that may be required is an intensification and an orchestration of sentiments and of ÔÔframingsÕÕ that many people are already at least moderately sympathetic toward. We might think of ideology as an explicit cultural modelÑbetter orga- nized than the various components of tradition and culture (Swidler, 1986). That is, individuals may have an initially un- systematic array of sentiments (such as unconnected views about how bad the current situation is, how useful violence can be, and what constitutes a sacred value) but this array is transformed into a more coherent system by way of some ide- ology that provides a unitary frame and a compelling story-line. The system may be held together more by this compelling narrative than by the ideologyÕs internal logic. In the composite narrative identified here, a tragic crisis has arisen due to vio- lations of sacred values by an evil and inhuman enemy and a glorious mission that includes resorting to violence is a way to redeem and rectify the situation. On the basis of this model for understanding militant extremism, the strength of the fanatical thinking pattern should erode to the extent that the degree of the crisis, the sacredness of the mission, and/or the violations of sacred values are shown to be exaggerated, and the argument for violence as a necessary response is undercut."
text_normalised: Narrative is a compelling storyline that transforms an initially unsystematic array of sentiments, views, and values into a more coherent system by providing a unitary frame. It organizes disparate cultural and traditional components into an explicit cultural model, holding the system together through its compelling quality rather than through strict internal logic. A narrative structures disconnected elements—such as perceptions of crisis, attitudes toward action, and conceptions of sacred values—into a unified account that makes sense of situations and prescribes responses. The coherence and persuasive power of narrative derive from its ability to integrate various sentiments and framings into a single, meaningful story that participants find resonant and motivating, rather than from logical consistency alone.

text: "Terrorist groups such as al Qaeda perceive that their identity is threatened, and believe that the only way to remove that threat is by reconnecting with their heroic past. The myth provides a narrative that encourages group members to engage in ÔÔGodÕs workÕÕ against the oppressor in order to destroy the threat and regain past heroism to achieve a glorious future." "Understanding the underlying symbolic pattern facilitates taking steps to prevent the message from spreading. Ordinary people do not normally strap on suicide vests or fly planes into buildings; it is essential to identify the symbolic transformation that leads to such acts. In this essay, we argue that the symbolic DNA of the terrorist message is a mythic symbolic pattern that serves as both a persuasive and an epistemic device. Terrorists do not go through some sort of satanic transformation and suddenly become evil- doers. Rather, the most dangerous terrorist groups, including those carrying out mass-casualty attacks against civilian targets, rely on a mythic rhetorical pattern based in religion or an ideological/mythic system similar to religion. This pattern acts as a symbolic schema that legitimizes terrorism, transforming it into sacramental violence. Kenneth Burke labels this creation a terministic compulsion leading to violence (1966, 2003). This pattern is found among terrorists whose religious views are tied to all the major faiths. While our focus is on al Qaeda as an exemplar of the symbolic pattern, all of the religious and ideological/mythic terrorist groups tell a mythic narrative of how the group, whose very identity is threatened with destruction, can regain its strength, protect its culture, and defeat the evil enemy it faces by returning to the heroic virtues that were present at the creation of the groupÕs identity. To the outside world, the mythic system may appear absurd, but for a community of believers that is ÔÔintoxicated only by their ideologyÕÕ (Richardson, 2006, p. 15), it functions as what Malinowski called a ÔÔreality livedÕÕ (1954, p. 100), producing transformation into a ÔÔdivinely inspired armyÕÕ (Richardson, 2006, p. 150). The remainder of this essay first explains the theoretical rationale behind the position that religious/ideological terrorists are motivated by a terministic compul- sion to use violence to cleanse the world of evil, then outlines the symbolic DNA of terrorism itself, before demonstrating its application to the most important terrorist group operating in the world, al Qaeda, and finally shows how an understanding of the symbolic DNA of terrorism has important implications for preventing the further spread of terrorism." "Mythic/ideological symbol systems are especially powerful because they serve as totalistic devices for explaining the world, providing a sense of identity, and putting the individual in touch with the transcendent. A myth is a fundamental story, what Doty referred to as a ÔÔspecialÕÕ or ÔÔbigÕÕ story ÔÔtouching not just the everyday but sacred or specially marked topicsÕÕ (1986, p. 8) in a society. A myth in this sense is not a false story, but is a true story that is ÔÔbelieved in one sense or another by the people who tell itÕÕ (Rowland & Frank, 2002, p. 26). Because myths tell stories of the actions of heroes who are larger than life, often operating in special places possessing great symbolic power, such as heaven, hell, or Jerusalem, at times that are endowed with great meaning, such as the beginning or ending of a culture or a time of great crisis (Eliade, 1963; Rowland, 1990), they provide a sense of ÔÔtranscendent grounding for any societyÕÕ (Rowland & Frank, 2002, p. 26). Although not all myths are religious, in a sense they all are sacred for they take us out of the here and now to a place and time where transcendent deeds may be done and an ultimate truth discovered. It is for this reason that powerful ÔÔsocial movements, which must motivate millions of people to act, are nearly always mythicÕÕ (p. 27); a sense of the sacred is needed to motivate mass action. Even the most secular of mass movements, Marxism, had at its core the myth of a workerÕs paradise to come (Halle, 1965)."
text_normalised: A narrative is a story that explains the world, provides a sense of identity, and connects individuals to transcendent meaning. It functions as both a persuasive and epistemic device, serving as a symbolic schema that shapes understanding and motivates action. Narratives are grounded in mythic or ideological systems that tell fundamental stories about heroes, significant places, and meaningful times—such as moments of creation, crisis, or cultural transformation. These stories are believed by those who tell them and operate as "reality lived," offering totalistic frameworks for interpreting experience. By linking present circumstances to heroic pasts and envisioned futures, narratives legitimate particular courses of action and facilitate symbolic transformation. They are especially powerful in motivating collective behaviour because they invoke sacred or specially marked topics that transcend everyday experience, providing transcendent grounding for communities and movements.

text: "This article explores martyrdom mythologies in Iraq by drawing extensively on the literature of jihadists since the beginning of the Iraqi insurgency.1 These include video clips,2 audio recordings,3 biographies of suicide bombers,4 online magazines,5 and still images posted online.6 Special emphasis is given to how jihadists portray the fallen ÔÔmartyrs.ÕÕ By elevating the suicide bombers to the status of extraordinary moral beings who make the ultimate sacrifice for God and the Muslim nation, jiha- dists deflect attention away from their atrocities and the victims they harm. It must be made clear from the outset that the portrayal of bombers in video clips and biogra- phies is highly propagandistic and in all likelihood does not reflect the totality of their motivations. The point of focusing on martyrdom mythologies is to show how groups seek to achieve several communicative goals through manipulation of narratives, not to suggest that these mythologies reflect the true motivations of the suicide bombers. The latter is a complex research question that falls outside the scope of this article."
text_normalised: Narratives are communicative constructions employed by groups to achieve specific goals through the strategic manipulation of accounts. They function as tools for shaping perception and meaning by selectively presenting information in ways that advance particular objectives. In this capacity, narratives can deflect attention from certain realities while elevating other elements to prominence. They operate as propagandistic devices that may not reflect underlying truths or complete motivations but instead serve instrumental purposes in persuasion and influence. Groups utilize narratives to portray events, actors, and circumstances in manners aligned with their communicative aims, constructing versions of reality that support their strategic interests rather than necessarily representing factual totality.

text: Narratives and stories can serve as a general metaphor for understanding human conduct. In part this is so because people think in narratives about their own lives. text: "In the context of a manifesto, they are all stories that articulate defences to violence that are prevalent in society, but are applied in ways that are neither recognised nor accepted as valid by society."

Narratives thus operate at the intersection of available cultural repertoires and their unconventional deployment, bridging familiar justificatory frameworks with applications that transgress established boundaries of legitimacy. They represent attempts to make sense of and defend actions by invoking societal logics while simultaneously challenging or subverting the conventional limits of those logics' applicability.

text: After the 9/11 attacks, terrorism has become one of the most sought-after and covered topics in the news. Different studies have shown that the media play an important role in constructing narratives about perpetrators and victims of terrorism, and can influence public opinion about these events and thus shape responses to counter-terrorism policies (Bradshaw & Kenski, 2019; Iyer et al., 2014; Krugman, 2001; McDermott & Zimbardo, 2007; McGregor et al., 2005; Saleem et al., 2015; Schmuck et al., 2021; Washburn & Skitka, 2014). Moreover, although terrorist attacks often result in a limited number of direct victims, media outreach has the potential to transform these events into collective trauma that affects the global community (e.g., Bar_Tal & Labin, 2001; Legewie, 2013). Empirical evidence confirms that news media consumption after terrorist attacks is linked with stronger support for strict measures against terrorism, such as military intervention in third countries (Bradshaw & Kenski, 2019; McGregor et al., 2005; Saleem et al., 2015; Washburn & Skitka, 2014), restrictive immigration policies (Mythen & Walklate, 2006; Saleem et al., 2015) and securitization measures that come at cost of personal civil liberties (e.g., being identified by the police or allowing the government to monitor e-mails and phone calls, Greenberg et al., 2004). p. 375
text_normalised: Narratives are media-constructed accounts about perpetrators and victims of events that influence public opinion and shape responses to policies. These constructions have the potential to transform events with limited direct impact into collective experiences that affect broader communities. Through their presentation and framing, narratives can be linked with support for specific measures and policy positions, demonstrating their capacity to influence attitudes and responses at a societal level. Narratives function as interpretive frameworks through which events are understood and given meaning, mediating between occurrences and their reception by audiences, thereby shaping collective understanding and subsequent reactions.

text: "Narrative media interventions, also referred to as edutainment, weave messages into a story Òto both entertain and educate, in order to increase audience membersÕ knowledge about an educa- tional issue, create favorable attitudes, shift social norms, and change overt behaviorÓ (Singhal et al., 2004, p. 5). Narrative interventions use storytell- ing to effect change. Different from communica- tion strategies that use direct persuasive techniques through providing information, the audience gets immersed in the story, identifies with its charac- ters, and, for a short time, vicariously experiences the fictional reality and emotions of the characters (M. C. Green & Brock, 2000). The audienceÕs identification with the characters and transporta- tion to the imaginary reality reduce resistance and possible counterarguments that are typical of more direct persuasive attempts (e.g., Murrar & Brauer, 2019; Slater & Rouner, 2002). Narrative interventions, such as serial dramas delivered through media, have been used successfully to induce behavior change in domains including health (Wakefield et al., 2010), poverty (La Ferrara, 2016), corruption (Blair et al., 2019), gender-based violence (D. Green et al., 2020), prejudice (Murrar & Brauer, 2018; Paluck, 2009), or intergroup rec- onciliation (Bilali & Vollhardt, 2013)."
text_normalised: A narrative is a story that conveys messages by immersing audiences in a fictional reality where they identify with characters and vicariously experience their emotions. Unlike direct persuasive communication that provides information explicitly, narratives engage audiences through storytelling, creating transportation into an imaginary world. This immersive quality reduces resistance and counterarguments typical of overt persuasive attempts. Narratives can be delivered through various media formats and may be designed to educate audiences, create favorable attitudes, shift social norms, and change behavior by leveraging character identification and emotional engagement rather than direct argumentation. The defining features are the story-based structure, audience immersion in a fictional reality, character identification, and vicarious emotional experience that distinguish narratives from non-narrative forms of communication.

text: "Beyond an individualÕs personal experience while engag- ing in collective action, judgments of the ingroupÕs past col- lective action experiences should also influence group membersÕ engagement in action. Participants in collective action might receive cues from the media and public discus- sions about the effectiveness of their actions. Accordingly, participants might become more or less involved in future action depending on their personal experience during collec- tive action (e.g., Tausch & Becker, 2013), and the publicÕs and mediaÕs framing of the actions as success or failures. Similarly, observers of collective action who are sympathetic to its goals, but have not yet become involved, may be more or less likely to join in collective action in the future based on their percep- tions of the movementÕs past successes and failures (Beckwith, 2015; Stuart et al., 2018). We build upon Freel and BilaliÕs (2022) theorizing that narratives of past success and failure of collective action efforts should influence group membersÕ tendency to engage in collective action and its psychological drivers, including efficacy beliefs, hope, and anger."
text_normalised: Narratives are accounts or framings of past collective experiences—such as successes or failures of collective action—that are communicated through media and public discussions. These accounts provide cues about the effectiveness or outcomes of group efforts and shape group members' perceptions of their ingroup's history. Narratives influence psychological states, including efficacy beliefs, hope, and anger, and thereby affect individuals' likelihood of engaging in future collective action. They function as interpretive frameworks that both participants and sympathetic observers use to evaluate past events and inform subsequent involvement in collective efforts.

text: "The high level of social mobilization against migrants in Italy, manifested through actions that are often illegal or violent, presents a critical area of investigation. At the heart of these wide- spread sentiments are the political and symbolic discourses fueled by right-wing parties and movements. These groups capitalize on anger and anxiety, positioning themselves as defend- ers of the so-called native silent majority. Media messaging, particularly via social networks, poses an important tool for the radical right to distribute such narratives effectively and gauge broader support. This study delves into how such narratives impact societal attitudes and be- haviors toward migrants. In particular, it examines how cultural homogeneity within radical political groups and media representations of migrants influences the propensity for political violence among Italy's political rights supporters. This inquiry is situated within a complex landscape where political attitudes toward migration intersect with phenomena such as politi- cal violence, anti-democratic behavior, and social mobilization."
text_normalised: Narratives are political and symbolic discourses employed by groups to shape societal attitudes and behaviors. They function as communicative tools distributed through media channels, particularly social networks, to convey specific framings of social issues and gauge support. Narratives operate by capitalizing on emotions such as anger and anxiety, positioning particular groups in relation to others within society. They serve to influence how individuals and collectives perceive and respond to social phenomena, including shaping propensities for action. Narratives intersect with political attitudes and can be strategically deployed to mobilize constituencies around contested issues. Their impact extends to affecting behavioral outcomes and social mobilization patterns within populations exposed to these discursive constructions.

text: "Misinformation is defined as the inadvertent sharing of false information (Ireton & Posetti, 2018), and it is generally accepted that consuming misinfor- mation can influence individualsÕ likelihood of being radicalized (Davies, 2021). Significant strides have been made in defining what constitutes misin- formation (vs., ÒdisinformationÓ; Baines & Elliott, 2020), the types of material that are often used in misinformation campaigns and the form and functions of online groups who spread misinformation (Cook et al., 2015). While there are complexities to defining and utilizing the term ÒmisinformationÓ with some scholars disavowing the overarching use of the term (Baines & Elliott, 2020), we are increasingly aware of the many and varied forms of harmful forms of online media. While misinformation is defined as false or misleading informa- tion that is not necessarily intended to deceive), disinformation is defined as false and misleading information provided with the intention to deceive. Malinformation is authentic information provided with the intent to cause harm (Omoregie, 2021). However, it is important to denote that the inherent problem of these definitions is that they define the content based on the motivation of the sender and not the perception of the viewer. In this article, misinformation will be defined as false information that is presented as true (see Cook et al., 2015). This is not to be confused with other types of information such as disin- formation, which is when information is deliberately created to be deceitful (Bained & Elliot, 2020)."
text_normalised: Misinformation is false information that is presented as true. It differs from disinformation, which involves information deliberately created to be deceitful, and from malinformation, which consists of authentic information provided with intent to cause harm. A key limitation of traditional definitions is that they classify content based on the sender's motivation rather than the viewer's perception. Misinformation can take many and varied forms of harmful online media and may be disseminated through campaigns utilizing specific types of material and through online groups. While complexities exist in defining and utilizing the term, and some scholars question its overarching application, misinformation is generally distinguished by its presentation of falsehood as truth, regardless of whether deception was intended by those sharing it.

text: "To be clear, in this paper, we define conspiracy beliefs as the act of considering a conspiracy theory to be a trustworthy source of information. It is important to distinguish this concept from related terms such as conspiracy theories and conspir- acy mentality. Conspiracy theories are specific frameworks that often contradict available evidence and propose alterna- tive explanations for events or situations. Meanwhile, con- spiracy mentality is the individual predisposition to explain events as conspiracies (Imhoff et al., 2022a, b)." "The narrative, as a further element in the 3N model, reflects the ideological beliefs of one's group. Embracing social narratives imparts a sense of value and belonging within a meaningful universe to individuals (Solomon et al., 2004). Serving as a cultural worldview, narratives are employed by individuals to ascribe meaning to their own existence and life experiences (Pyszczynski et al., 2015). They not only offer individuals a sense of belonging but also prescribe appropriate behaviors, ensuring their membership and self- esteem within a specific social context. In this vein, within the 3N model, the narrative plays a pivotal role as it serves as a compass, delineating what is socially important, and secondly, it provides guidance on the methods to achieve those priorities (Kruglanski et al., 2018). Narratives can encompass diverse ideological beliefs, whether religious or secular, such as Christianity (Vancs, 2020), Islam (Stoja- rov & Stojar, 2019), environmentalism (Riedel, 2021), or animal rights (Lucardie, 2020), just to name some. Any nar- rative can function as an ideological guide for individuals and groups, influencing their understanding of themselves and their social context, and sometimes steering them toward radicalization (Webber et al., 2020). Within the 3N model of radicalization, believing in con- spiracies theories corresponds to subscribing a narrative that justify and promote political violence (Kruglanski et al., 2022c). While not always explicitly advocating for vio- lence, such beliefs often embody the two key ingredients of a violence-justifying ideology: a grievance and a culprit (Kruglanski et al., 2014). These elements identify both a wrong committed against one's group and the perpetrator deserving of punishment (Webber et al., 2020), fostering an antagonistic mindset that can fuel intergroup conflict. Furthermore, conspiracy theories, often built around power dynamics (Butter & Knight, 2020), create a starkly divided worldview with opposing factions: the oppressive elite and the oppressed majority of people. This sense of victimhood (Pantazi et al., 2022) can spark retaliatory actions to reclaim perceived social standing, which the believers feel has been diminished by the supposed conspirators. Consequently, those subscribing to conspiracy theories may perceive themselves as unfairly targeted by a powerful and mali- cious group, potentially justifying violence as a response to this perceived injustice (Ardvol_Abreu et al., 2020). Since humans rely on a fundamental need for mutual understand- ing and a shared perception of reality (Echterhoff et al., 2009), the legitimacy of the any set of values reflecting in beliefs (namely, an ideology, see Jost et al., 2009) justifying extreme commitment must be shared to be validated (Web- ber & Kruglanski, 2016). Hence, the narrative most effec- tively meeting the need for significance is the one endorsed by a social network significant to the individual."
text_normalised: A narrative is a framework of ideological beliefs that reflects a group's worldview and serves as a cultural compass for individuals. It functions to ascribe meaning to existence and life experiences, providing individuals with a sense of value, belonging, and membership within a meaningful social context. Narratives delineate what is socially important and prescribe appropriate behaviors and methods to achieve group priorities. They can encompass diverse ideological beliefs—religious or secular—and influence how individuals and groups understand themselves and their social environment. To be validated and effectively meet psychological needs, a narrative must be endorsed and shared by a social network significant to the individual, as humans rely on mutual understanding and shared perceptions of reality.

text: "As participants confront a loss of identity at the moment of disengagement from the group, and the new challenge of identity reconfiguration through stop-gap measures, they must also invariably come to terms with the past. There is an increasing temporal divide that now stretches between oneÕs previous identity as an extremist and oneÕs new alternative and developing identity. The problem, according to our analysis and model, is that some participants get stuck in a temporal loop, re-living their past narratives in various ways rather than moving toward a new future and a transformed identity (Fisher Smith et al., 2020). This is also another point at which participantsÕ core need becomes particularly salient, emerging in this moment of identity crisis to direct behavior. Of course, participants were not aware of a core need per se, but rather, their immediate struggles to make sense of the past."
text_normalised: Narratives are temporal constructions through which individuals make sense of their past experiences and identities. They function as cognitive frameworks that can either facilitate or impede identity transformation, particularly during periods of significant life transition. When individuals attempt to reconfigure their sense of self, narratives serve as mechanisms for processing previous identities and experiences. However, narratives can become repetitive patterns that keep individuals psychologically anchored to past identities rather than enabling forward movement toward new self-conceptions. In moments of identity crisis, narratives emerge as sense-making tools through which individuals attempt to reconcile temporal divides between former and developing identities. The construction and reconstruction of narratives represents a fundamental process through which people negotiate the relationship between their past experiences and their evolving sense of self.

text: The distinct narratives of white supremacists, incels, political extremists, and those with personal grievances, coupled with their shared themes of alienation and disenchantment, highlight the complex interplay between individual grievances and broader ideological convictions. This nuanced understanding is pivotal for both law enforcement and mental health professionals, informing strategies that address the specific and collective pathways to violence (page 15)
text_normalised: Narratives are accounts that articulate individual grievances and broader ideological convictions, characterized by themes such as alienation and disenchantment. These accounts reflect a complex interplay between personal experiences and collective belief systems, creating pathways that connect individual circumstances to wider ideological frameworks. Narratives serve to express and potentially justify positions or actions by linking personal dissatisfaction with systematic worldviews. They function as vehicles through which individuals situate their experiences within larger interpretive structures, bridging subjective grievances and shared ideological perspectives. Understanding narratives requires attention to both their specific content and their collective thematic elements, as they operate simultaneously at individual and group levels to construct meaning and coherence.

text: Utilizing natural language processing, we aimed to identify distinct linguistic patterns and thematic elements inherent to each group, as well as uncover overlapping narratives of disenfranchisement and aggression. p. 3  Consistent with existing literature (Anti-Defamation League, 2018; Byman, 2021; Reyna et al., 2022), our analysis shows that white supremacist texts reveal a distinct thematic focus that differentiates them significantly from other extremist groups. Unlike incels, whose grievances are more personal and introspective, and political extremists, who are driven by systemic concerns, white supremacists embed their ideologies in broader historical, racial, and cultural narratives (Anti-Defamation League, 2018; Byman, 2021). Their discussions often revolve around concepts of European heritage, fertility rates among white populations, and the Great Replacement Theory Ð a conspiratorial belief that white people are being systematically replaced by non-white populations through migration and demographic changes (Ekman, 2022). These topics are not merely rhetorical; they are deeply embedded in a narrative that seeks to justify acts of violence as a form of defense or preservation of white identity (Anti-Defamation League, 2018; Jess & Pierre, 2020). p. 10  The shared discourse among these groups provides a narrative through which members can rationalize radicalization as a political statement or necessity (Treistman, 2024). p. 12  When considering the overlap among all three ideology groups Ð white supremacists, incels and political extremists Ð themes of death, killing, fear, emotions, human nature, conformity, religion, hate, and happiness become pronounced. These themes reveal a collective fixation on mortality, control through violence, and an emotional spectrum that is heavily influenced by fear and hatred (Hoffman et al., 2020). Conformity and religion often serve as justifications for their ideologies, while discussions on human nature and happiness reflect a yearning for a sense of purpose and identity within a like-minded community (Hoffman et al., 2020). Such shared narratives across these ideologies underscore the role of fundamental human emotions and psychological needs in the radicalization process (Blanger et al., 2019). p. 12  Attackers driven by personal grievances are motivated by personal experiences of injustice, frustration, or interpersonal conflicts (Lankford, 2018). Their writings reflect narratives of perceived slights, focusing on direct grievances (Blanger et al., 2019). In contrast, ideologically motivated attackers frame their actions within broader socio-political narratives (Ajil, 2022; Byman, 2021). p. 12  The distinct narratives of white supremacists, incels, political extremists, and those with personal grievances, coupled with their shared themes of alienation and disenchantment, highlight the complex interplay between individual grievances and broader ideological convictions. p. 15
text_normalised: Narratives are thematic and linguistic frameworks through which individuals and groups articulate ideologies, grievances, and justifications for beliefs or actions. They embed specific concerns within broader historical, cultural, or socio-political contexts, providing coherent structures that rationalize positions and behaviours. Narratives serve to justify acts, including violence, by framing them as necessary responses to perceived threats or injustices. They enable members of communities to construct shared meaning, fostering collective identity and purpose through common themes and emotional appeals. Narratives can be personal, focusing on individual experiences of injustice or conflict, or ideological, situating actions within systemic or conspiratorial interpretations of social phenomena. Shared narratives across groups reveal overlapping themes—such as alienation, fear, and mortality—that reflect fundamental psychological needs and emotional states. Through discourse, narratives facilitate the rationalization of radicalization and provide frameworks for understanding human nature, conformity, and belonging within like-minded communities.

text: Although previous work by Obaidi et al. (2022) has already shed light on the radicalising effects of the GRC, we contend that this phenomenon requires a more nuanced investigation. This is mainly because Obaidi et al. (2022) examined only one version of this conspiracy theory, namely the Muslim conspirator version. When investigating this version of the GRC, it is reasonable to focus exclusively on radical tendencies against Muslims because this version accuses all Muslims of being a unified antagonistic entity, moving to Western countries with the ultimate goal of establishing global dominance through an Islamic order (Obaidi et al., 2022; Swami et al., 2018; Uenal et al., 2021). As a result, exposure to such a narrative may serve as a justification for engaging in radical actions against Muslims (also see Sutton & Douglas, 2022) (page 4)
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that presents events, actors, and causal relationships in a way that frames a particular interpretation of social reality. It identifies specific groups or entities, attributes intentions and actions to them, and constructs a coherent storyline about their roles and objectives. Narratives can assign collective identities to groups, portraying them as unified actors with shared goals, and may position these groups in relation to others, including as antagonists or threats. By organizing information into a meaningful framework, narratives shape how individuals understand social phenomena and can influence attitudes and behavioral responses. They may provide interpretive schemas that justify particular courses of action by establishing perceived legitimacy for responses to the situations or groups depicted within the narrative structure.

text: "This study investigates the psychological, ideological, and networking factors that predict harmful attitudes and beliefs among self-identified incels. We draw upon the 3N theory of radicalization (Kruglanski et al., 2019, 2022; Webber & Kruglanski, 2017), which conceptualizes radicalization through three interconnected factors: Needs, Narrative, and Network. Needs reflect an individual's psychological driv- ers, such as mental health issues or a need for significance. Narrative encompasses the ideological beliefs that justify grievances and violence, and Network refers to the social connections that reinforce these narratives. The 3N model has been validated in several contexts (Blanger et al., 2019; Milla et al., 2022), demonstrating how individual motivations, ideological narratives, and social support systems interact to drive extreme behaviors. For instance, Gonzlez et al. (2022) found that indicators of each of the three factorsÑNeeds, Narrative, and NetworkÑwere present in individuals convicted of terror offenses. Ellenberg et al. (2023) applied the 3N framework to a sample of self- identified incels, identifying three subtypes of incels: hopers, internalizes, and externalizers. Externalizers, characterized by strong support for violence, were particularly influenced by their lack of a supportive network (social isolation) and their admiration for incel perpetrators. These findings high- light the utility of the 3N model in explaining incelsÕ harmful attitudes and behaviors."
text_normalised: Narrative encompasses ideological beliefs that justify grievances and violence. Within frameworks of radicalization, narrative represents the cognitive and ideological dimension through which individuals interpret their circumstances, attribute blame, and rationalize extreme attitudes or actions. Narratives provide explanatory frameworks that legitimize perceived injustices and may sanction harmful responses. These belief systems interact with psychological drivers and social networks to shape attitudes and behaviors. Narratives function as sense-making structures that connect individual experiences to broader ideological positions, offering coherence to grievances and potentially justifying violence or other extreme conduct. The concept emphasizes the role of belief systems in translating personal or collective dissatisfaction into ideologically framed positions that support radicalization processes.

text: "Specifically, we  conceptualize ÒneedÓ as the search for meaning, ÒnetworksÓ as deviant associations, and ÒnarrativeÓ as criminal attitudes" "Engaging in criminal behaviors typically hinges on the offender holding favorable attitudes toward the specific behavior or justifying it (Akers, 1998). Similarly, radical behaviors are strongly predicted by radical attitudes, which involve positive evaluations of violence to further a cause (Wolfowicz et al., 2020). As previously mentioned, beliefs about the legitimacy of violence are often deeply embedded in the group the individual belongs to such as a criminal gang or a terrorist group. Within these groups, other members validate and reinforce the narrative, rewarding individuals with respect and admiration for adhering to its principles (Kruglanski et al., 2019). While radicalization research has largely concentrated on attitudinal outcomes, resulting in the development of diverse tools to measure and support radical attitudes, criminology has primarily prioritized behavioral outcomes. Nevertheless, several measures of criminal cognition have been developed, such as the Psychological Inventory of Criminal Thinking Styles and the Measure of Criminal Attitudes and Associates scales. Although these validated instruments and their subscales have proven highly beneficial, they often blend various cognitions with attitudes. These cognitive components frequently encompass thinking styles like impulsivity or moral disengagement, while attitudes primarily refer to evaluations or orientations toward offending behaviors."
text_normalised: Narrative consists of attitudes that evaluate or orient individuals toward specific behaviors, particularly those involving violence or rule violation. These attitudes include favorable evaluations of the behavior itself or justifications for engaging in it. Narratives are embedded within and reinforced by the social groups to which individuals belong, where other members validate and reward adherence to these attitudinal frameworks through respect and admiration. The concept encompasses evaluative orientations toward behaviors rather than broader cognitive components such as thinking styles, impulsivity, or moral disengagement mechanisms. Narratives function as shared belief systems within groups that legitimate particular courses of action, providing both cognitive frameworks for understanding behavior and social validation for those who adopt them.

text: Understanding how social media platform architecture molds user decisions and experiences is an important consideration in responding to far-right extremism. Far-right extremists have resonated with one anotherÕs content using features available within FacebookÕs platform interface. These design features afford users with a range of possible behaviors and experiences. Features such as the emoji-like ÔReactionsÕ available to users when responding to posts, for example, are designed to grant users a simple and economical means to communally resonant with posted content. When this content is extremist in nature, however, it becomes important to understand how platform affordances, such as the use of ÔReactionsÕ, influence user interpretation of the themes and narratives depicted (page 352)
text_normalised: Narratives are thematic depictions of content that can be interpreted by users. They are elements that can be presented through media platforms and are subject to user interpretation. Narratives convey themes that may vary in nature and can be responded to or engaged with through platform-mediated interactions. The interpretation of narratives is influenced by the affordances and features of the communication environment in which they are encountered. Narratives exist as content that users process and make sense of within specific communicative contexts.

text: First, to operationalize the notion of extremist narratives and understand the shared narrative patterns of the two protest movements, we draw on BergerÕs (2018) definition of extremism as a spectrum of beliefs, rather than a simple or Ôfixed destinationÕ (p. 68). Drawing on social identity theory, he argues that whether violent or nonviolent, extremist movements revolve around the same Ôvalue propositionÕ, which holds that the extremist in-group offers a solution to a threat-based crisis that is rooted in the existence of an out group. We take cues from his work to understand extremism as Ôthe belief that an in-groupÕs success or survival can never be separated from the need for hostile action against an outgroupÕ (2018, p. 44). Here, hostile actions might designate a range of behaviors, from discriminatory behavior, hate speech, and harassment to violence and even genocide. At the heart of all extremist ideologies and movements then, are narratives fleshing out identity constructions around the demarcation of ingroups and out-groups, and around crisis-solution constructs based on those group-identity definitions (page 166)
text_normalised: Narratives are structured accounts that elaborate identity constructions by demarcating in-groups and out-groups, and that articulate crisis-solution frameworks based on those group-identity definitions. These narratives flesh out belief systems by establishing boundaries between social groups and by linking the in-group's success or survival to the existence of a threatening out-group. They provide the conceptual architecture through which movements articulate value propositions, positioning the in-group as offering solutions to crises rooted in out-group presence. Narratives thus serve as vehicles for expressing ideological positions that revolve around group-based identity distinctions and threat-response constructs, organizing beliefs around the relationship between collective identity, perceived threats, and proposed resolutions.

text: "In this study, we aim to address this lacune by examining right-wing extremist parentsÕ beliefs and narratives about childrenÕs ideological socialization in the context of the online community Stormfront. Analyzing right-wing extremist parentsÕ first-hand accounts allowed us to gain insight into their Ôreal-timeÕ opinions and perspectives on childrenÕs upbringing, and the ways in which they socialize them into their violent worldviews. To do so, we conducted a qualitative analysis of Stormfront usersÕ parental narratives. Inherent to narrative analysis is the idea that all communication ultimately comes down to the telling and sharing of stories, which in turn reveal how we understand ourselves and the world around us (Herman & Vervaeck, 2019; Presser & Sandberg, 2019). Narrative analysis is therefore concerned with uncovering the implicit or explicit accounts that individuals use to make sense of their life experiences (Maruna & Liem, 2021; Presser & Sandberg, 2019). This approach has in recent years proven fruitful in understanding engagement in violent extremism and processes of radicalization more generally (Copeland, 2020; Ferguson & McAuley, 2020; Lakhani, 2020). In the current study, we maintain that narrative analyses are equally suitable to understand right-wing extremistsÕ approaches to family life and their respective ideas on the ideological socialization of children. These insights are useful for all individuals working with families in which children are potentially raised with right-wing extremist ideas and may aid in the development of adequate prevention and intervention measures in the long run."
text_normalised: Narratives are communicative forms that consist of the telling and sharing of stories through which individuals reveal their understanding of themselves and the world around them. They comprise implicit or explicit accounts that people use to make sense of their life experiences. Through narrative analysis, these stories can be uncovered to reveal how individuals construct meaning from their experiences and perspectives. Narratives serve as vehicles through which people communicate their worldviews, beliefs, and interpretations of reality. They are fundamental to all communication and provide insight into how individuals perceive and organize their experiences into coherent frameworks of understanding.

This implies that a narrative must contain some sort of action, even if there is only one action undertaken. This definition implies that a narrative must contain some form of action, even if minimal, as the absence of events would result in a description, exposition, or argument rather than a narrative. More specifically, narrative constitutes the symbolic presentation of a sequence of events. The representational nature of narrative distinguishes it from direct experience, positioning it as a mediated account that conveys occurrences through symbolic means. The sequential dimension is central, as narratives organize events in temporal or causal relationships. This framework applies across contexts, encompassing any symbolic representation that depicts actions or occurrences, regardless of their factual status or thematic content.

text: Existing theories of radicalization can be roughly divided into three kinds with respect to their treatment of ideology and narrative. Some theories of radicalization suggest that narratives alone can be enough to move individuals to radical action, for example if these narratives appeal to Ôsacred valuesÕ culturally salient ideas that members of the culture are willing to kill and die for (Atran & Sheikh, 2015), or to mortality salienceÑa reminder or a threat of death that triggers a cultural anxiety buffer that allows an individual to deal with the existential terror by actively supporting the outgroup and denigrating or aggressing against the outgroup (Pyszczynski et al., 2009). Other theories postulate no causal role of narratives, contending that social connections and group dynamics are responsible for radicalization, and ideology comes secondary to the motives to support the network or a small face to face groups with intense interpersonal ties (Sageman, 2004). Finally, some theories of radicalization suggest that narratives can lead to radicalization if and when they coincide with other radicalizing factors such as social networks or psychological motivations or needs (Hafez & Mullins, 2015; Kruglanski et al., 2022; McCauley & Moskalenko, 2008). Supporting the idea of synergistic motivational interactions between narratives and other factors, McGregor et al. (2015) proposed that aggressive religious radicalization is spurred by a combination of factors including conducive personality traits such as high anxiety and low agreeableness, conducive threats including seemingly insurmountable external forces, and conducive affordances including opportunities for immediate and concrete engagement in active groups and narratives justifying political violence. In short, ideology and narrativesÕ role in radicalization remains debated and understudied (McCauley, 2024). In terms of their content, a variety of radicalizing narratives are studied in terrorism and political violence research. Most commonly mentioned are grievances: individual or group views of injustices perpetrated against individuals, group, or ideas with which one identifies (Moghaddam, 2005). Another radicalizing narrative is a narrative of hate (McCauley & Moskalenko, 2016; Valeri & Borgeson, 2016). Narratives that radicalize through eliciting hatred capitalize on psychology of essentialization, a belief that the enemy all share some bad and unchangeable essence (Haslam, 2006). Essentialization of the outgroup can lead to dehumanization of that group, which manifests in describing its members as animals, beasts, diseases, or vermin (Haslam, 2006; Haslam et al., 2002). The logical implication of essentialization and dehumanization is that the only remedy for the bad essence is complete eradication: to kill the beast, to exterminate the vermin, or to cut out the disease. This rhetoric marked the Nazi propaganda leading up to the holocaust against Jews in 1930s Germany; it also characterized the lead-up to the Rwanda genocide, and it can be found in communications of terrorist groups such as Weather Underground in the 1970s US and PeopleÕs Will in the 1870s Russian Empire when these groups describe their enemies (Moskalenko & McCauley, 2020). Historically, minority groups such as Jews, Roma, women, and LGBTQ have been represented in conspiratorial narratives as inhuman or subhuman (Bloom & Moskalenko, 2021; Moskalenko & Romanova, 2022). Recently, RussiaÕs President Putin announced in a 2023 televised address to the Russian nation that ÔWestern curators put an ethnic Jew at the head of UkraineÕ to Ôcover up the anti-human essenceÕ of modern Ukraine (i24NEWS, 2023), demonstrating how antisemitism and essentialization of the enemy can be combined into conspiratorial and potentially radicalizing narratives. pp. 1-2  Conspiracy theories are generally defined as explanatory beliefs about a group of powerful actors that collude in secret to reach malevolent goals (van Prooijen & Douglas, 2018). This malevolent group may consist of people (e.g. politicians or company owners, see Pirro & Taggart, 2023) or even non-human entities (e.g. human-lizard hybrids, see Lewandowsky & Cook, 2020). p. 3  Although there are conceptual disagreements on what constitutes narrative (Moskalenko, Freilich et al., 2023), definitions tend to converge on the idea that narrative can be defined as the representation of an event or a series of events (Abbott, 2008; Altman, 2008). This implies that a narrative must contain some sort of action, even if there is only one action undertaken. Without an event, one could compose a description, an exposition, an argument, or some combination of these, but one could not rightfully compose a narrative (Braddock, 2012). Scholes (1981) defined narrative as Ôthe symbolic presentation of a sequence of eventsÕ (p. 205). Genette (1982) echoed ScholesÕs claim, Ôone will define narrative without difficulty as the representation of an event or sequence of eventsÕ (p. 127). Although relatively little attention has been paid to the narrative structure of conspiracy theories, numerous studies recognize that conspiracy theories rest on a strong narrative foundation (Raab et al., 2013; Tangherlini et al., 2020). Following this, and the definitions above, we will refer to conspiracy theories as conspiratorial narratives, because they describe symbolic representations of events, namely, malevolent actors conspiring to cause harm to specific victim groups. Conspiracy theories are unique among political narratives in that they may represent a symbolic threat rather than a Ôrealistic group conflict,Õ such as conflict over land, resources, or power (Sherif, 1988), or a contested social identity (Tajfel & Turner, 2010). This makes conspiracy theories particularly interesting as possible stimuli to radicalization: if indeed they are capable of inciting radicalization by mere exposure, this must be attributed to the narrative itself, as opposed to the narrativeÕs representation of real worldÕs conflict. Thus, conspiracy theories offer a unique opportunity to delineate the political effects of narratives, specifically whether they might contribute to radicalization. pp. 4-5  By combining the two kinds of conspiratorial narratives (QAnon and Russian propaganda) we also want to test whether peopleÕs reactions to them would differ Ð suggesting the content of the narrative is important, or be more consistent Ð suggesting the general conspiratorial nature of the narrative is what people respond most to. p. 7
text_normalised: Narrative is defined as the representation of an event or a series of events, constituting a symbolic presentation of a sequence of occurrences. This definition implies that a narrative must contain some form of action or event; without such events, one produces a description, exposition, or argument, but not a narrative. Narratives serve as symbolic representations that can convey explanatory beliefs, describe conflicts, or present sequences of actions undertaken by actors. In the context of social and political psychology, narratives may represent real-world conflicts over tangible resources or contested identities, or they may present symbolic threats through their representation of events. The structure and content of narratives allow them to function as vehicles for conveying beliefs about actors, their motivations, and the consequences of their actions, though the specific mechanisms by which narratives influence attitudes and behaviors remain subject to theoretical debate.

text: "I define narrative as the construction of social meaning by making present life experi- ences or understandings of the world (Schiff, 2012) through (implicit or explicit) connec- tions between two (or more) events (Copeland, 2019), where characters within the story can influence its development and outcome (Richardson, 2002).6 GottschallÕs (2021, p. 19) illustration of the power of story and narrative to influence human thinking enriches this definition by providing the purpose of narrative."
text_normalised: A narrative is the construction of social meaning by making present life experiences or understandings of the world through implicit or explicit connections between two or more events. Within this construction, characters can influence the story's development and outcome. Narratives serve to influence human thinking by organizing events and experiences into meaningful patterns that shape how individuals and groups interpret reality. This definition encompasses both the structural elements—linked events and agentive characters—and the functional dimension of meaning-making that operates at social and cognitive levels.

text: We contend that TrumpÕs alliance with QAnon symbolized a shift from presidents appealing to God to presidents becoming a messiah in a political religion, in this case through the acceptance of a millennialist narrative fashioned by the fringe conspiracy movement that portrayed the president as their Savior. More than just solidifying his base by uniting the evangelical right with antigovernment conspiracy theorists, the move was significant for the way it weaponized conspiracy theories against democratic communication. (page 683)  Extending this notion of conspiracy rhetoric as weaponized political communication, we contend that Donald TrumpÕs embrace of QAnon marked the rise of what we call presidential eschatology. In simplest terms, eschatology is theÒconcept of dealing with the end of all material and purpose in time and spaceÓ (White, 2001, p. 938).Fenster (2008) explained that popular eschatology is the practice of providingÒan accessible and comprehensible, all-encompassing narrative frame or metanarrative that can explain the past, the present, and the future for a mass audienceÓ (p. 198). Eschatological rhetoric, specifically with regard to Christian interpretations, uses religious stories, allegories, figures, and themes to construct a picture of what the world will look like when Christ returns and ushers in the apocalypse. (page 684)
text_normalised: A narrative is an accessible and comprehensible, all-encompassing frame or metanarrative that explains the past, present, and future for an audience. It provides a coherent structure through which events, conditions, and temporal sequences can be interpreted and understood. Narratives may employ stories, allegories, figures, and themes to construct a picture of reality and its trajectory. They function as organizing frameworks that render complex phenomena intelligible by situating them within a broader explanatory structure. Narratives can be fashioned by groups or movements and may be adopted or endorsed by individuals in positions of authority. They serve to unite audiences by offering shared interpretive resources and can be deployed as forms of political communication. The comprehensiveness of narratives allows them to integrate diverse elements into a unified account that orients understanding across temporal dimensions.

Through this dual function of highlighting what is socially significant and legitimating specific behaviors or decisions, narratives serve as vehicles for transmitting normative information within groups or communities. They operate by making explicit connections between valued principles and recommended conduct, thereby framing how individuals should understand and respond to situations.

Narratives create roles and expectations and serve as a central point in understanding the construction of personal and collective identity and behavioral patterns. They also build a shared meaning of the past, present, and future to shape the behavior of domestic and international actors (page 266, 267)
