text: This paper addresses a significant gap in how links between conspiracy theories and violent extremism can be conceptualised by terrorism researchers and counter-terrorism practitioners, and how these links can be tested empirically through forms of structured textual analysis. Expanding research methods in this area offer new insights into the diverse ways conspiracy theories can motivate violent extremists and terrorists, and act in some cases as drivers for violent acts against outgroups. Better clarifying the link between conspiratorial language and violent acts will also assist in providing opportunities for improved detection of mobilising emotions and language within conspiratorial narratives online useful to policy makers, counter terrorism practitioners, and social media companies (page 1, 2)
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured form of communication that can contain conspiratorial language and mobilising emotions. Narratives function as vehicles through which ideas, beliefs, and motivations are expressed and transmitted, particularly in online contexts. They possess identifiable linguistic and emotional characteristics that can be detected through structured textual analysis. Narratives can serve to motivate individuals or groups toward particular actions or attitudes, including those directed against outgroups. The structured nature of narratives allows for systematic examination of their content, language patterns, and emotional dimensions, making them amenable to empirical investigation and analysis by researchers and practitioners seeking to understand their influence on behaviour and attitudes.

text: Three theoretical frameworks provide the basis for the analysis: (1) The presence of conspiracy theory elements (agency, coalition, threat, secrecy), (2) radical narrative constructs (crisis, solution, justification), and (3) mobilising emotions (anger, contempt, disgust Ð ANCODI). (abstract) Two types of source text were analysed in this study, an original conspiracy theory and three far-right shooter manifestos that claim to be influenced by it. Original conspiracy theory: The Great Replacement (sometimes simply termed ÔreplacementÕ) narrative is an anti-migrant, white nationalist conspiracy theory stating that political elites are complicit in the purposeful demographic replacement of white European populations with non-European peoples through migration, demographic growth, and declining ÔwhiteÕ birth rates (Bracke & Hernndez Aguilar, 2020; Campion, 2019; Obaidi et al., 2022). In its more extreme forms, it claims that this immigration process is part of a plot to emasculate white populations and engineer a white racial genocide (Wilson, 2018). The narrative was popularised by French academic Renaud Camus in his short 2011 self-published book Le Grand Remplacement (Williams, 2017), although the concept dates back to a 1916 article by American eugenicist Madison Grant, The Passing of the Great Race (Grant, 1916), which influenced the German Nazi Party. A related concept was also expressed in the ÔEurabiaÕ narrative which explicitly posits that Muslims are overtaking Europe, and which was cited repeatedly in the 2011 far-right manifesto produced by Anders Breivik (van Buuren, 2013; Zia-Ebrahimi, 2018). In 2018, Camus self-published an English version of his book entitled You Will Not Replace Us! This text was selected in this study as providing the empirical source of the Great Replacement conspiracy theory in its most basic form because Camus directly controlled its translation between French and English, and because its concepts were cited in the later manifestos. p. 4 Pre-attack manifestos: The three manifestos used in this study were each penned by violent extremists prior to undertaking their attacks. p. 5 In 2019, three violent attacks by individuals holding extreme far-right views prominently featured pre-attack manifestos documenting the attackerÕs justification, explanation, influence, and recruit for their cause (Ehsan & Stott, 2020). These were the Christchurch attack by Brenton Tarrant in March (The Great Replacement), the Poway attack by John Earnest in April (An Open Letter), and the El Paso attack by Patrick Crusius in August (The Inconvenient Truth). (A fourth attack was conducted in October, by Stephan Balliet who attempted a mass casualty incident at a synagogue in Halle, Germany). Each conducted an ideologically motivated violent attack aimed against a non-white minority; Muslims in the case of Christchurch, Jews in the case of Poway, and Hispanics in the case of El Paso. The Poway and El Paso attacks and manifestos were influenced by the style and success of the earlier attack in Christchurch, which was designed to go viral and achieved significant spread through social media (Waldek et al., 2021). Each manifesto explicitly referenced the Great Replacement conspiracy theory and used it to justify violence against a perceived Ônon-whiteÕ outgroup. As written artefacts composed prior to engaging in violence, these manifestos provide a unique opportunity for analytical comparison between an original conspiracy theory and later pieces of propaganda designed to justify and promote a terroristic attack against an outgroup (Table 1). p. 5
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured account that presents a sequence of events, claims, or ideas to convey a particular interpretation of reality. It organises information into a coherent framework that can include elements such as identified agents, perceived threats, proposed crises, and suggested solutions. Narratives may incorporate conspiracy theory components (agency, coalition, threat, secrecy) and radical constructs (crisis, solution, justification). They can be disseminated through various textual forms and may reference or build upon earlier narratives. Narratives serve to frame social, political, or demographic phenomena in ways that support specific ideological positions, potentially providing justification for attitudes or actions toward identified groups. They can be transmitted across languages and contexts, influencing subsequent iterations that adapt or extend the original framework while maintaining core conceptual elements.

text: "Pauline Boss (2006) has recommended narrative intervention to address ambiguous loss. Narra- tive therapy can be considered a poststructural- ist form of therapy positioned within the social constructionist domain of social psychology, and premised on the idea that the lives and the relationships of per- sons are shaped by: the knowledges and stories that communities of persons negotiate and engage in to give meaning to their experiences: and cer- tain practices of self and of relationship that make up ways of life associated with these knowledges and stories. A narrative therapy assists persons to resolve problems by: enabling them to separate their lives and relationships from those knowl- edges and stories that they judge to be impover- ishing; assisting them to challenge the ways of life that they find subjugating; and, encouraging persons to re-author their own lives according to alternative and preferred stories of identity, and according to preferred ways of life. (Dulwich Cen- tre, quoted in Besley, 2001, p. 127)"
text_normalised: Narratives are knowledges and stories that communities negotiate and engage in to give meaning to their experiences. These narratives shape the lives and relationships of persons, forming practices of self and relationship that constitute ways of life. Narratives are socially constructed within communities rather than existing as fixed, objective accounts. They provide frameworks through which individuals interpret their experiences and construct their identities. Narratives can be impoverishing or subjugating when they constrain persons' understanding of themselves and their relationships. Alternatively, narratives can be re-authored according to preferred stories of identity and ways of life. The meaning-making function of narratives operates through social negotiation and engagement within communities, establishing the interpretive frameworks that organize personal and relational experience.

text: " Past research on meaning in life highlights the importance of meaning frameworks that provide individuals with a sense of confidence and understanding of their reality. More importantly, meaning frameworks not only describe how the world generally opera
text_normalised: Narratives are meaning frameworks that provide individuals with a sense of confidence and understanding of their reality. They describe how the world generally operates and prescribe how individuals should act within it. Narratives function as interpretive structures that help people make sense of their experiences and guide their behavior by offering both descriptive accounts of reality and normative prescriptions for action. These frameworks enable individuals to organize their understanding of the world while simultaneously providing direction for how they ought to engage with it. By combining descriptive and prescriptive elements, narratives serve as comprehensive sense-making tools that address both the "is" and "ought" dimensions of human experience, allowing individuals to navigate their social and psychological environments with greater coherence and purpose.

text: "The predominant idea we observe among this current IIHGT threat is best described as the Ôglobal jihadist narrativeÕ, and the components we have outlined above are embedded within this idea. It identifies a serious problem related to how society is organized and pre- scribes a solution to remedy the challenges. This, ultimately leads to a new society which will be just and perfect."
text_normalised: A narrative is a structured idea that identifies a problem in how society is organized and prescribes a solution to remedy that problem, ultimately leading to a vision of a new, improved society. It functions as a framework that embeds and organizes multiple components into a coherent account of social challenges and their resolution. The narrative presents both diagnostic and prescriptive elements: it articulates what is wrong with the current social order and offers a pathway toward transformation. This structure enables the narrative to serve as a comprehensive ideational system that connects present grievances to future aspirations, providing both explanation and direction for social change.

text: "Narrative criminology explores the ways that Ôpeople estab- lish who they areÑtheir identity workÑby emplotting their experienceÕ into narratives (Presser 2012: 6). Attention to narrative has been a mainstay across many disciplines, from history, to literature, to psychology and to anthropology, and while narrative criminology derives from these diverse traditions (Presser 2009), it is distinguished by a commitment to an analysis of the ways in which narratives themselves are constitutive antecedents of crime. Constructionist in nature, narrative criminology conceives of narratives as an Ôontological condition of social lifeÕ and pushes discursive analysis to the forefront of concern (Somers 1994, cited in Presser 2009: 184), rather than dwelling on Cartesian dualisms implicit in deliberations about the extent to which narratives are artful impositions of subjectivities onto ÔrealÕ events, or analyses of how narratives neutralize what is ÔactuallyÕ morally suspect behaviour."
text_normalised: Narratives are accounts through which people establish their identities by emplotting their experiences into structured forms. They constitute an ontological condition of social life, serving as discursive frameworks that shape understanding and action. Rather than being mere retrospective impositions of subjective meaning onto pre-existing events, narratives function as constitutive elements that actively structure social reality. They operate beyond simple representations or post-hoc rationalisations, instead forming fundamental conditions through which individuals construct who they are and interpret their lived experiences. This conceptualisation emphasises narratives as primary social phenomena requiring analysis in their own right, rather than as secondary reflections of underlying objective realities or as strategic devices that merely reframe morally problematic behaviour after the fact.

text: "The Fnix Andaluca program is based on the 3N model of radicalization (Kruglanski et al., 2019; Webber & Kruglanski, 2017), which proposes that radicalization arises from the intersection of three psychological forces: need, narrative, and network. According to this model, the process begins with a loss of significance (or an opportunity to gain it), which leads to a quest for significance (Kruglanski et al., 2022). This need triggers a collectivist shift, whereby the individual in question seeks narratives that tell him or her how to recover significance (Kruglanski et al., 2019). In turn, the narrative adopted must be validated by a reference group, which will provide the significance sought, as long as the individual adopts the narrative (Kruglanski et al., 2018). In the case of violent extremism, narratives legitimize violence as a means of achieving personal significance (Webber et al., 2020). The 3N model postulates that these three factors contribute to radicaliza- tion in a dynamic and interactive manner (Kruglanski et al., 2019). Although the order of factors may vary (Blanger et al., 2019; Lobato et al., 2020), the most studied pathway begins with a loss of significance, focusing on the ref- erence group and adopting its violent narrative. For instance, Adam-Troian et al. (2020), Bck et al. (2018), and Milla et al. (2022) found that the signifi- cance loss was related to greater support for violent narratives, and this effect was mediated by the presence of a deviant network. The authors tested this with students, the general population, and terrorist samples."
text_normalised: Narratives are cognitive frameworks that prescribe courses of action for individuals seeking to fulfill psychological needs, specifically by indicating how to recover or attain personal significance. These frameworks must be validated by a reference group to confer the significance sought, contingent upon the individual's adoption of the narrative. Narratives function as meaning-making structures that connect individual motivations to collective ideologies, providing direction for behavior. In contexts involving extremism, narratives may legitimize specific means, such as violence, as pathways to achieving personal significance. The adoption of narratives represents a collectivist shift wherein individuals turn to shared belief systems that offer solutions to psychological deficits or opportunities for gain. Narratives operate dynamically and interactively with other psychological and social factors in shaping individual orientation and commitment to particular courses of action.

text: As groups polarize and fragment, changes in narratives mirror the changes in the group membersÕ shared beliefs, values, including moral convictions, and norms about group behavior. That is, changes in the social identity content of the group. To illustrate our argument, we consider how collective narratives may vary at different phases of transformation, using dissent about the value of cultural diversity in society as an example. For someone aligned with a center-right ideology, this may mean voting for an anti-immigration politician. Those identifying with a more extreme faction may support harsh immigration policies and enforcement methods (a more extreme narrative). At the furthest extreme, individuals may endorse or engage in violence against minority groups. This progression illustrates how increasingly radical narratives can lead to more extreme attitudes and behaviors. (page 4)
text_normalised: Narratives are structured accounts that reflect and embody a group's shared beliefs, values, moral convictions, and behavioral norms—collectively constituting the social identity content of that group. As groups undergo polarization and fragmentation, their narratives transform correspondingly, mirroring shifts in these shared elements. Narratives exist along a continuum of extremity: moderate narratives align with centrist positions, while increasingly radical narratives correspond to more extreme attitudes and behaviors within progressively radicalized factions. These narrative variations demonstrate how the content and intensity of collective accounts scale with the degree of group polarization, ranging from conventional political positions to endorsement of extreme actions. Narratives thus serve as dynamic representations of group identity that evolve as the group's ideological boundaries shift and intensify.

text: "Simply put, a narrative is a Òsystem of storiesÓ that Òrelate to one another.83 Stories are Òpieces that can come and go, change, and morph,Ó but the overall narrative remains.84 Extremist groups may employ a combination of religious, ideological, moral, and political narratives that could be based on a combination of facts and half-truths, and comprising real or imagined stories of grievances, injustices and mistreatment.85 In response to Islamist extremist narratives, governments around the world have been developing Counter-Narratives and Alternative Narratives. These are types of strategic communications with the aim of informing, educating, and reforming targeted audi- ences. Counter-Narrative and Alternative Narrative projects can include fact-checked information products, awareness campaigns, and community outreach programs con- ducted via a combination of printed, digital, and face-to-face platforms. At the time of writing there appears no clear consensus amongst academics and practitioners on widely agreed-upon definitions of Counter-Narratives and Alternative Narratives. Some analysts employ ÒCounter-NarrativeÓ as a broad and catchall term or see Alternative Narrative efforts as an aspect of a larger Counter-Narrative policy. Kate Ferguson thus observes that Òcurrent CVE [Countering Violent Extremism] literature and policy concerned with countering propaganda is dominated by the language of Ôcounter-narrativesÕ yet a common understanding of this relatively new lexicon has not emerged.Ó
text_normalised: A narrative is a system of stories that relate to one another. While individual stories within this system are pieces that can come and go, change, and morph, the overall narrative remains stable. Narratives may employ combinations of religious, ideological, moral, and political elements. They can be based on combinations of facts and half-truths, comprising real or imagined stories of grievances, injustices, and mistreatment. The system's coherence derives from the relational connections among its constituent stories rather than from the permanence of any single story, allowing the narrative to persist even as specific stories within it are modified or replaced.

text: "In the context of social movements research, framing refers to what Benford and Snow call the Òmobilization and countermobilization of ideas.Ó18 Frames are rhetorical strategies intended to motivate action. By examining the frames a movement utilizes, we can infer a great deal about the values and worldview that prevail within the movement and its social environment, since organizations strive to frame issues in a manner favorable to their own mission and interests.19 Furthermore, this process of selecting and broadcasting certain frames to the exclusion of others necessarily represents a continuous negotiation between an organizationÕs leadership and its membership base.20 For example, Babb demonstrates that collective frames Ð however sophisticated and carefully crafted Ð will fail to resonate if they fundamentally contradict the lived experience of the population they are intended to influence.21 Additionally, frames evolve in response to Òcounter- framesÓ put forward by competing actors, giving rise to situations where frames function as semantic weapons in a contest of adversarial meaning production.22 Empirically speak- ing, analyzing how a movement frames its activities affords us insight into what themes and arguments the leadership thinks will most resonate with their followers and with the masses they are attempting to influence.23"
text_normalised: Narratives are rhetorical strategies employed to mobilize ideas and motivate action within social contexts. They function as frames that organizations select and broadcast to align with their mission and interests, reflecting the values and worldview of both the movement and its broader social environment. The construction and dissemination of narratives involves continuous negotiation between leadership and membership, as effective narratives must resonate with the lived experiences of their intended audience to succeed. Narratives evolve dynamically in response to competing counter-narratives, operating as semantic instruments in contests of meaning production between adversarial actors. Through their strategic deployment, narratives reveal which themes and arguments are deemed most persuasive for influencing followers and broader populations, making them key sites for understanding collective mobilization and ideological contestation.

text: "To be most effective, such frames ought to resonate with Òmaster framesÓ which have Òmobilizing potencyÓ contingent upon their Ònarrative fidelity.Ó22 In other words, master frames draw on broader pre-existing cultural narratives such as Òextant beliefs, myths, folktalesÓ23 that are well known to the group. They therefore rely on existing norms and narratives to enable otherwise diverse groups of people to suspend their differences and band together.24 One key master frame frequently deployed by social movements is that of religion, which Òprovides ready-made symbols, rituals and solidarities that can be accessed and appropriated by movement leaders.Ó25 Scholars have demonstrated that the master frame of religion fulfils various functions within social movements: it legitimizes certain behaviors; it creates a unified set of moral and social norms that are tightly adhered to by the faithful; and it provides a rich tapestry of symbols and scriptures, of heroes and martyrs, and a belief in a higher purpose.26 There is also a significant body of literature that demonstrates the extent to which political elites deliberately manipulate and selectively utilize religion as a mobilization frame, transforming the faithful into a partisan political force which enables the elites to promote their agenda, achieve political goals, and even be elected to office.27 Religion, therefore, Òdrapes a powerful sacred canopy over the sometimes banal, some- times brutal work involved in political mobilization.Ó28 The master frame of religion can also serve as a powerful mechanism to mobilize towards acts of political violence, including random acts of terror.29 Here, Mark Juergensmeyer refers to Òcosmic war,Ó in which the leaders of key religiously based social movements sacralize their political struggles in order to give their movement an aura of legitimacy and justify the use of violent means.30 Indeed, religion has been shown to be a more effective way to mobilize individuals towards political violence than other salient identity markers such as ethnicity.31"
text_normalised: Narratives are pre-existing cultural stories, including beliefs, myths, and folktales, that are well known to a group and serve as foundational frameworks for interpretation and action. They provide a shared cultural repertoire that enables diverse individuals to suspend differences and unite around common understandings. Narratives supply ready-made symbols, rituals, and solidarities that can be accessed and appropriated. They establish unified sets of moral and social norms, offer rich tapestries of heroes, martyrs, and higher purposes, and legitimate certain behaviors. Narratives function as mechanisms through which leaders can mobilize groups by drawing on these familiar cultural resources, thereby lending legitimacy and coherence to collective endeavors. Their effectiveness depends on their resonance with the group's existing cultural knowledge and their capacity to frame specific situations within broader, recognizable story structures.

text: "One way to counter the TalibanÕs messages is to analyse its narratives of violence. Compared to the Cold War when governments had limited access to enemy data, militant groups have used the Internet to publish extensively, with massive data that few have analysed based on the linguistic skills needed to read these texts (Wagner, 2011). Militant groups use the Internet to change the thoughts, emotions, and behaviours of potential recruits and pre-existing con- stituencies (Bhui & Ibrahim, 2013). In an exhaustive meta-analysis of 298 studies that compared the thoughts, emotions, and behaviours of participants exposed to any type of narrative vs unexposed par- ticipants, psychologists of communication have found that: (1) narratives could be characterized as cohe- sive, casual, sequences of events resulting from the purposeful actions of protagonists, and (2) the beliefs, attitudes, and behaviours of participants exposed to such media start to align with messages in narratives (Braddock & Dillard, 2016). Effective counter-messaging strategies include exposing contra- dictions in militant narratives and the ways that mil- itants act with respect to such narrative, disrupting analogies that equate aspects of the narratives to real-world events and disrupting binary thinking in narratives (Braddock & Horgan, 2016). Given that the Taliban has used the Internet to disseminate periodicals since 1998 (Aggarwal, 2016), scrutinizing its narratives could present empirical data to custom- ize counter-messaging strategies."
text_normalised: Narratives are cohesive, causal sequences of events resulting from the purposeful actions of protagonists. When individuals are exposed to such structured accounts, their beliefs, attitudes, and behaviours begin to align with the messages embedded within these narratives. Narratives function as communicative tools that can influence the thoughts, emotions, and behaviours of audiences, including potential recruits and existing constituencies. They operate through coherent storytelling that links events causally and centres on intentional agents. The persuasive power of narratives lies in their capacity to shape cognitive and affective responses, thereby modifying how recipients think, feel, and act in relation to the narrative content.
